utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Obradovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The cross-examination by Mr. Stamp will continue. Please bear in mind that the solemn declaration which you made to speak the truth at the beginning of your evidence will continue to apply to that evidence today. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Good morning, General Obradovic.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'd like to return to where we left off today the issue in respect to the plan Grom 98, and I'll ask you to answer direct as you can so we could move on quickly. This is a matter that has been explored before in detail by questions from Mr. Ackerman and the Presiding Judge in respect to the witness General Vasiljevic, and I wish to give you a copy of the order in your own language and ask you a couple questions about it. This is 4D137. And I'll basically be going over just for the record questions that were asked by counsel and by the Court at transcript page 8917 and thereafter. You look at that order, General. If you look to the top right-hand corner, you see R. You see the Defence state secret followed by an R, Grom 98. If you look within it generally and if you look at page 2 of your copy in particular, which is page 3 in English, you will see various directives including this one: "Through quick action coordinating the forces of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia, overwhelm and destroy the sabotage and terrorist forces in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija as per a special order from the General Staff of the VJ." And later on on the same page you see the readiness in the deployment areas is 17 days upon receipt of the mobilisation signal at the latest. You recall this is dated the 28th of July. In response to questioning about that document, having had an opportunity to peruse it, General Vasiljevic said that it is a document pertaining to the war plan. It is a document of war planning how something is developed -- would -- would develop, I'm sorry. This is not an executive order to be implemented right away. The subordinate commands when they receive a directive such as this they draw up their own documents based on this, but the decision for the army to act on this as far as I can understand the situation and the rules such a decision cannot be issued by the General Staff and Chief of the General Staff by passing the institution superior to him, primarily the president of the state and the Supreme Defence Council. So this is an element of war planning, preparation for a certain situation. Do you agree with his characterisation of that document, that it is an element of war planning and it is not for execution?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The situation that we were facing in mid-1998 was quite complex both domestically and abroad, including Kosovo. Based on predictions and indicators, the inference could be drawn that an act of aggression or a war was foisted on the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. The plan was drawn up in order to deal with the sabotage and terrorist forces in Kosovo. In the latter half of 1998, there were a great many indicators pointing to the possibility of an aggression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Obradovic. Mr. Obradovic, you've been asked a technical question. You've not been asked yet about the circumstances which gave rise to this in this section of questioning. You're being asked whether this is a directive which is simply -- a part of the planning exercise which requires to be implemented later by specific orders. Now, can you answer at that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly. As the situation became more complex, it would be necessary to have additional order for stage two to deal with mobilisation. The manpower levels in peacetime were not sufficient for the eventuality of an aggression. There would have had to be a partial or full mobilisation, and for that to happen a particular state had to be declared, and this decision could only be taken by the Supreme Defence Council or alternatively the federal government.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So back to that document and back to the question I was asking. Now, do you agree that that was a document for war planning purposes, and it is not an executive order to mobilise for combat operations? Just focus on the document and the purpose of that document.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document was not directly related to entering the war. It was about dealing with terrorism in Kosovo. It was based on this plan and this directive that the anti-terrorist operation in Kosovo was run.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Obradovic, are you saying is you cannot answer the question, that it's framed in a way that makes it impossible to answer yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I answered to the extent that I understood the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you don't understand the question. Is that the position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not that I don't understand. I answered what I understood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, are you now satisfied with the answer you've had?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, I'm not, but.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're being asked what appears to me as layman to be a simple question, of whether this is actually an order to do anything or whether it's simply a statement of the plan on the basis of which specific orders were required to be given for action to be taken. Now, are we misunderstanding that as a simple question for an army officer in your position to answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is an order which once it had been passed and adopted took effect. There was no need for a special plan or order to start the anti-terrorist operation in Kosovo. When this plan was approved, it took effect immediately, and its implementation started.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When was it approved? In the sense of its implementation for mobilisation of operations would take effect.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you can see if you looked at the header of the directive, it was produced and rubber stamped on the 28th of July by the chief of General Staff, towards the end of July. And then there was the explanation of this decision by the commander of the 3rd Army to bring manpower levels up, and this happened on the 3rd of August, the beginning of August 1998. And it was pursuant to a decision of the commander of the 3rd Army that the plan took effect to all practical intents and began to be implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So you -- you are saying that you know of an order made by the chief of General Staff pursuant to Grom 98 authorising deployment for combat operations in July or August made pursuant, an order made pursuant to Grom 98. You are aware of such an order?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Combat operations, no, because the war had not begun yet. There was the anti-terrorist struggle in Kosovo, but that was in our country. Terrorism was rife, and the plan had the objective of crushing the terrorist forces as quickly as possible and as successfully as possible. There were indicators of course at the time that a full-scale aggression on our country from somewhere outside might soon occur.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You said just now that it would take effect on the 3rd of August. Can I ask you this then: Why?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. He didn't say anything about it taking effect on the 3rd of August. That's a mischaracterisation of the evidence. What he said is the 3rd Army commander issued some kind of an order on the 3rd of August, but that had nothing to do when it took effect. His evidence is it took effect immediately when signed by General Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you read lines 13, 14 and 15, please. Do you still maintain your objection? Just a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: What he said was there was an explanation of this decision by the commander of the 3rd Army to bring manpower levels up and that happened on the 3rd of August. And then it was pursuant to a decision of the command of the 3rd Army that the plan took effect. That decision was the 29th of August. We talked about it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that may be so, but you'll have an opportunity to resolve of this if you feel it's not been adequately explored in due course. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I wish to draw your attention to that portion of the transcript. I think the term "combat operations" was mistranslated into B/C/S and that might cause some confusion with the witness. It was translated as "war operations," but when the transcript is checked and looked at we can take care of that too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, but it is important because it -- it seems to have presented the wrong question to the witness. It may have been expressed as anti-terrorist activity rather than war or combat to make it absolutely clear that we're talking about. Please continue, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can I put it this way: Do you know of an order from the chief of the General Staff made pursuant to Grom 98 that you have there in your hands for the VJ to deploy for anti-terrorist activity in July and August?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the order by the Chief of the General Staff. This was issued in late July, and of course based on this order his subordinate commands assessed their respective situations in their areas. They take their decisions and the commander of the 3rd Army explained what he envisaged to the Chief of the General Staff on the 3rd of August, 1998. Once this was approved it immediately took effect and combat operations could now get underway against the terrorist forces in Kosovo. This is the gist of the plan that was drawn up in late July and rubber stamped early in August 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And that is what I was asking. Maybe I just don't understand the military terminology. You say the command of the 3rd Army explained what he envisaged the Chief of the General Staff on the 3rd of August 1998 once this was approved it immediately took effect and combat operations could get -- could now get underway against the terrorist force in Kosovo. How was this plan approved? This is what I want to know. Was there an order approving the plan so it could take effect? And where is that order?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In our system of command, the map would normally be drawn up and attached to any plan on how the forces were to be used. There would be a pictorial representation of how the tasks were to be carried out. So this decision was followed by a pictorial representation on a map showing how the forces would be deployed, in what areas, and what the axes of operations would be and what the task was that was to be accomplished.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In what form did this decision to deploy on the basis of Grom 98 take?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This had the form of an order. It was an executive thing, and one had to start carrying out these tasks immediately in order to combat terrorism.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Would it be a written order therefore? Would a written order be needed, therefore, for this decision to take effect?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we're talking at cross-purposes here for some reason. There was a directive that was submitted to the commander of the 3rd Army by the General Staff and this is the directive I have now have before me. The army command would then make certain assessments and see what the tasks were contained in the order received from the General Staff. Based on those tasks they would in their turn assess the situation at their own level the 3rd Army, what its role was, what its tasks were, and what the commander army had envisaged in terms of them carrying out this task. He would explain his reason to the Chief of the General Staff and the Chief of the General Staff would approve and actually sign the map off, the map that was attached to the order. He would sign it off, thus rubbing stamping his ideas on how the tasks were to be carried out. So this is the gist. In addition to the text orders are drawn up at this level, and as you can see the General Staff delivers directives. This -- this was under the rules on the exercising of command in the army. And normally within each document of this type there would be a huge topographic map showing all the units in all the areas with their tasks, the tasks that they were to be carrying out in future operations in the anti-terrorist struggle. And then the map would say at the top of the page, "I hereby approve this plan," and this was Perisic at the time, and this automatically meant that he issued in order.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note: We did not understand the last part of the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you repeat the last part of your answer, please. You said the map would say at the top I hereby approve of this plan, this was Perisic at the time. This automatically meant that he issued an order. Did you say something else after that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. In the upper-left corner of the map it said I hereby approve, Chief of the General Staff, Colonel-General Momcilo Perisic. As soon as he signed off this document and this document was a component of the order, this meant that the decision was approved and that one could not start with implementing the tasks. And this was part of the command system at all levels from the army's General Staff down through the corps and all the way down the chain of command to brigade level. This was always a component part of every written document and a map would normally be attached to any decision like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that mean that there should be a map accompanying this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This document of the 3rd Army command should contain an attachment, a topographic map, a decision of the commander to deploy forces in the area because the entire area of responsibility of the corps was present, and it was envisaged that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerman, this is your document. Is it incomplete?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the document is incomplete, but I'm quite certain we do have the exact map that he's talking about. We just sent it off for reduction recently. I don't think it will be available to us today but I could probably have it tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But the map exists I'm certain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now -- now, that document provides, I think, that the chief of the 3rd Army should submit his plans pursuant to that document in order to -- to complete the planning purposes, and with the leave of the Court I'd like to show you 4D140. This is not on the list that we had proposed or we had notified the Defence about, Your Honours. This was raised by learned counsel Mr. Ackerman when he objected yesterday and put on the record yesterday in the course of his objection. So I'd like to ask the witness a couple questions about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There seems to be no objection to that, Mr. Stamp. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: 4D140. This is a copy of the 3rd Army order prepared on the basis of the Grom 98 directive, and it's dated the 29th of July, 1990. Do you recall the Grom 98 the command of the 3rd Army was to submit his plan by the 3rd of August, and the evidence is that he submitted this on the 28th -- or sorry, the 29th of July. Have a look at it generally. It's a long document. You will see within it that it has no date to begin mobilisation, that although it is drawn up on the 29th of July there is no date for it to go into force, for the forces to mobilise. And General Vasiljevic was also shown that document and asked about it, and he said: "The stages are provided for here but there is no date saying when mobilisation is to begin. So these are preparatory elements so that when such a decision is issued the army has its plans ready. So the activities here are planned by stage but no time frame is provided." He further say -- said: "You can't see when this enters into force. You can only see when it was drawn up pursuant to what the General Staff issued previously, that is, the directive of the General Staff." And lastly, he said: "What I maintain is this -- or I maintain what I said before. This is an element of preparation. This is the planning stage for combat which is yet to be implemented. The decision to implement the order when it becomes an executive order and the time frame are missing." Do you agree with his characterisation of that document, that it is also a preparatory document for war planning and it is not an executive order?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Prosecutor, it's evident that this document is linked to the directive of the General Staff and it bears the same title, "Grom 98." The directives were signed on the 28th and delivered to the command of the army, and the command of the army immediately began considering and assessing the situation and prepared a document. This document was prepared to explain to the General Staff the plan which was to be explained on the 3rd of August. One couldn't wait to write the order on the 3rd of August. It was written a day later and prepared along with the diagrams, and it was approved and verified on the 3rd of August, and as soon as it was approved this order entered into force. Although the date is 29th of July, it practically entered into force when on the 3rd of August the Chief of the General Staff verified it. You cannot prepare an order in two hours' time. It is a strategic document which takes time to prepare. The anti-terrorist operation did not last just a day or two. It went on for a long time.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: There is one error in the transcript. Line 23 I think the witness mentioned 3rd Army commander of 3rd Army. It is not possible in the two hours to prepare. We miss couple words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In explaining, Mr. Obradovic, that you cannot prepare an order in two hours' time, did you mention who could not prepare it in two hours' time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not about who couldn't do it. When the command of the army received the directive from the Chief of the General Staff, the manner and the method of working was to study the directive to see what the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've answered my question. Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So it is your evidence, General -- is it your evidence that the Pristina Corps of the 3rd Army became deployed for anti-terrorist activities in Kosovo on the basis of that plan? And that is in June -- sorry, July, August 1998.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm speaking of the order of the command, but the Pristina Corps was engaged on the basis of this order, the one it received from the commander of the 3rd Army. As you can see, the commander of the 3rd Army explained his ideas to his superior officer, and then the commander of the Pristina Corps probably explained to General Samardzic, the commander of the 3rd Army. So there's a cause and effect relationship down the chain of command. And this was done on the -- pursuant to the order of the command of the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly ask the witness to speak a little slower.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just very briefly. I would like to ask the witness to slow down. We already have a lot of problems in the transcript, and if we have to keep rising every two minutes it will not help us to proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by the leave page 13, line 25. The witness said and it's missing here and then the commander of the Pristina Corps acted on the orders he received from the commander of the 3rd Army. That's not what it says here, but that's what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Obradovic, the interpreters have indicated some difficulty in keeping up with your pace, so it would be helpful if you could speak a little more slowly. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And the question is and I think it --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And, General, the question is this: You're saying therefore that the Pristina Corps deployment and operations for anti-terrorist purposes in Kosovo in August and thereafter, 1998, was on the basis of this Grom 98 plan. Can you answer that with yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Are you aware, General, of a meeting convened by President Milosevic at Beli Dvor, at the palace, I think you know what I'm speaking of, in June 1998, to discussion preparations for a plan of action, anti-terrorist action in Kosovo, that was attended by General Perisic among other members of the army? Are you aware of that meeting? ?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Are you aware of one in July 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As I said, I was the chief of staff of the 2nd Army. I was not a member of the General Staff at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must object. What was that meeting in June in Beli Dvor that is being referred to? Can you give us a reference for June?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It has now been clarified as July.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, first he said June and then he asked about July as if there were two meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: My impression was he had made a mistake in the first part of the question. What is the position, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The second question. July is the correct month.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He made a mistake in saying June, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. But it must be reflected in the record. Page 15, line 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So you would not be aware of those meetings because you were at that time posted in the 2nd Army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you now saying there were two meetings?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: There were two meetings but I'm really asking him about one meeting in July.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You would not be aware of that meeting in July because you were in the 2nd Army at the time?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about any of those meetings. As I said at the outset, in the second half of July I was appointed to the General Staff before that, and I had been in the General Staff of the 2nd Army. I had been the chief of staff there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you have a date for that meeting, Mr. Stamp?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: 20th of July is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What was the date that your appointment to the General Staff took effect, Mr. Obradovic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I reported on the 10th of July to the Chief of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It would appear that the meeting took place after that date, but you're not aware of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the day I reported for duty, as I had been transferred from Podgorica I asked the Chief of the General Staff to give me five or seven days to settle some private problems of accommodation and so on. My family had stayed behind in Podgorica so that officially I began working on the 17th of July, 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the meeting was on the 20th, but you're not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that's correct. I'm not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we return to -- to P2166. This is a meeting on the 29th of October at Beli Dvor, convened by President Milosevic, attended by, as I told you earlier, General Perisic, General Dimitrijevic, General Samardzic, General Pavkovic, among others from the army. And General Pavkovic said what I read to you before but to remind I'll just read it again: "Speaking on behalf of the Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija, General Pavkovic reminded the members of the operation staff that the plan for suppressing terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija had been carried out in five stages." Firstly, you recall that the Grom 98 plan called for two stages, or two phases? You recall that? That answer calls for a yes or no. If you do, you do, if you don't, you do not?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to the directive at the level of the General Staff it was defined that the task should be implemented in two stages.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And according General Pavkovic the plan that it they had been working on had an overall duration of 45 to 55 days and that implementation of the plan commenced on the 25th of July, 1998, and activities planned were completed on the 28th of October, 1998. Now, were you aware of this plan carried out in five stages set for 45 to 55 days commencing on the 25th of July and completed on the 29th of October?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In connection with the document shown me, the minutes, I was not familiar with this document before arriving here, so I only saw it here for the first time. I was not familiar with it before. The minutes of the operative staff meeting allegedly held on the 29th of July.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: October, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that doesn't deal with the question. Is your answer to the question no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was answering the question as to whether I'm familiar with this document. I never had an opportunity of seeing this document before, before my proofing here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You may have misunderstood. You were asked if you were aware of a plan being carried out in five stages over a period of 45 to 55 days between the 25th of July and the 29th of October. Now, are you aware of such a plan or are you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not aware of any such plan. The subordinate commands when they receive a task at the operative strategic level can implement the order in more than one stage. If the superior commander says the plan should be carried out in two stages, the lower-level commands, in accordance with the actual situation, can break it down into more stages. So what matters is that the assigned task should be completed successfully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: While you were at the Joint Command, by October your job would be to know what the VJ -- would involve knowing what the VJ was doing operationally and how it was preparing -- sorry? I'm sorry, I withdraw that. Well, since I commenced Joint Command, can I just ask you, do you know of an organ referred to as a Joint Command in the latter part of 1998 and that the record here indicates that Mr. -- That General Pavkovic was speak on behalf of it? Do you know of the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, as I dealt mostly with these problems in the organisational scheme of commanding the army, there was no such institution. Nowhere did such an institution appear either linked to the General Staff or going up or down the chain of command of reporting, so that this institution you refer to as the Joint Command did not exist. The General Staff did not either receive or issue any documents in connection with that or orders, so my answer is completely negative.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, this is what the president's record says General Pavkovic was speaking on behalf of. So your answer is you don't know what General Pavkovic was speaking about when he spoke on behalf of the Joint Command? And that can be a yes or no. You do know or you don't know what General Pavkovic was speaking of when it is recorded here he spoke on behalf of the Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, whenever any of us put a question in this way you always said that it was speculation. The man never saw the document. He has no idea about this, and now he has to know what General Pavkovic meant when he spoke, if he spoke, and what he thought. You did not allow us to put such questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That is not a question which depends on speculation. That is a question which depends on the witness's knowledge of a body referred to in what appeared to be -- what appears to be an official record of things said by an accused here, and it's easy for him to tell us what his knowledge of that is, whether he knows what General Pavkovic is speaking about or not. So please answer the question, Mr. Obradovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My answer, Your Honour, is that in the organisational structure of command there was no Joint Command. What I --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. I take it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let the witness complete that answer. Please continue with your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that in the organisational structure of command from the highest to the lowest level nowhere in any documents did a Joint Command appear in General Staff documents, and in the chain of reporting upwards nowhere was a Joint Command mentioned. Such activities -- there were no activities of the General Staff relating to such a body or vice versa. That's the essence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Obradovic, does it concern you that in this record there is reference to a senior army officer talking about the Joint Command and you have no knowledge of such a body?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I am telling you what I know. I'm telling you about information I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand that, but the army is all about discipline, about people in authority knowing what has happened, unless there is a very good reason why they shouldn't. So can I ask you the question again. Does it not concern you that this record appears to record a senior army officer talking about an organisational body that you were unaware of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did my best to know what I had to know in the sector I was in charge of, and I think I was successful in this. What other people knew beyond that in other areas I couldn't say. The Chief of the General Staff should know most about this, and I suppose this question should be put to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You were sector Chief of Operations, staff affairs. Isn't it right within your bailiwick, within your capacity, to be aware of and monitor the deployment and operations of the various units of the VJ?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the sector inter alia we had the task of knowing the most important elements of what was being done in the commands at all levels. The subordination went downwards so that the General Staff knew what the army commanders as their immediate subordinates were doing, and the lower-level commanders reported to their superiors. The higher level did not get involved in the tasks of the lower level. There were several degrees of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: As sector chief for operations, staff affairs, your particular area of work within the Joint Command involvement planning and monitoring operations, the deployment of the VJ -- sorry, I withdraw that question and ask --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we can read General Staff. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your job involved planning for the deployment and monitoring the deployment of the units of the VJ. I think you said that. And I think you'll agree with me that in 1998 the most important deployment of the VJ was in Kosovo. So that being the case, you're saying that by October 1999 you were not aware of an anti-terrorist operation involving the Pristina Corps of the 3rd Army that began on the 25th of July, was scheduled for 45 to 55 days, and was brought, according to General Pavkovic, to a successful conclusion on the 29th of October. You're not aware of that plan?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, before the witness answers it was October '98, but it was interpreted as October 1999. So that might cause confusion.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Prosecutor, the term "Joint Command" is one I would ask you not to use in questions to me, because I was in charge of planning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I accept that, General, and please forgive me when I did and if I do. I hope I won't do it again. I just want to confirm this clearly. You are not aware of the plan I just asked you about?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I studied the document shown to me, the report General Pavkovic submitted, it covers mostly activities from the Grom 98 plan, the conducted of an anti-terrorist operation in Kosovo. The main tasks that at some meeting which I've already said I did not know about, but one can conclude that the gist of his report referred to the fight against the terrorist forces and that this was covered by the Grom 98 plan from the General Staff down the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've been able by reading the document to help us with that. Can you now help us with what might have been referred to as the Joint Command? If this is the Grom plan, which is what you think, and Mr. Pavkovic's report is on behalf of the Joint Command, can you help us with who he might have been reporting on behalf of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My answer is as follows: This body which existed in Kosovo, some kind of coordinating body or operative staff, that was apart from the army. There were some institutions there in Kosovo. There was the army, the police, the Ministry of Defence, the civil authorities, the civilian sector, and so on. So basically in the report, as I understood it and what General Pavkovic said as the corps commander, this all referred to the anti-terrorist operation conducted in the summer of 1998 on the territory of Kosovo and Metohija, and his report or whatever you want to call it fits into the activities ordered by the General Staff in the Grom 98 plan and not a plan of some sort of Joint Command, because as I said, in the organisational scheme there is no such thing as a Joint Command in the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Were you aware then of a coordinating body or operative staff that was apart from the army? And I'm using your words in asking you that specific question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did hear that there was a body down there in Kosovo dealing with those problems, everyday life, that kind of thing. However, I wasn't much interested in that body. Therefore, I can't give you any sort of complete answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The plan that General Pavkovic is speaking about could not fit within the Grom plan, the Grom 98 plan, could it, because according to you that was approved on the 3rd of August when General Pavkovic was speaking about a plan, the implementation of which started on the 25th. That is, the plan would have been approved -- would have been drafted and approved before the 25th of July. So it could not fit into the Grom 98 plan that you speak about, could it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The gist of the implementation of the tasks from Grom 98 is what General Pavkovic is saying. Was there another plan unrelated to this one from the General Staff? I certainly wasn't aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's move on. Thank you, General, for your answers. Can we look quickly at a document you were shown by learned counsel, 3D757. I'll just get page 11 in the English. Thank you. And that is at the top of page 14 in the B/C/S version of it. This is a report that you were shown. It was issued by General Perisic on the 1st of October, 1998, and the part I would refer you to is that part numbered 2 in which he says near the end of this report: "In future align the use of the VJ with the provisions of the constitution and the law, and the main precondition for the use of the VJ has to be declaration of one of the following states: State of emergency, immediate threat of war, state of war." That was what he inserted into his report on the 1st of October, 1998. Was this the consistent position of General Perisic?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is something that the Chief of the General Staff presented, because if what could be envisaged eventually followed, and you've seen the analysis, you've seen the overall assessment, and from an international point of view the situation was very serious, and very soon there could be a serious deterioration. And I think the Chief of the General Staff, and he was perfectly within his rights, that's what I believe, is saying here that should an aggression occur, the peacetime structure in the army could not be used to respond to all these challenges. There had to be a mobilisation, and there had to be a wartime plan for the use of the army. So he said should there be a radical change or even an act of aggression, we should under the constitution and the law declare one of these states, a state of emergency or a state of an imminent threat of war for the army to make it possible for the army to face that kind of situation. I think that is the fundamental idea behind what the Chief of the General Staff is saying here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Wasn't this position that there should be a state of emergency declared for the armed used of the VJ in Kosovo, this consistent position during 1998? That is what I was asking.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand what you mean in terms of him being consistent or inconsistent.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That he maintain this position without change, that there ought to be declared a state of emergency for the use of the VJ in Kosovo, a deployment of the VJ in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, the activities that were implemented were implemented within the framework of the Grom plan. However, the situation was becoming more and more complex, and you see the General Staff using the term in -- in the future. So should the situation become even more complex, then there is the eventuality that a state of war was to be declared so that a mobilisation could be conducted and the army could be prepared for what could follow. I think that is the gist of this argument, and I think I'm being perfectly clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. But what I'm asking you is not what he might have said about the future. What I'm asking you, was it his position in 1998 that there ought to have been a declaration of a state of emergency in Kosovo for the deployment of the VJ there? Was that his position?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you base your question on. This position of the General Staff is certainly clear to me. I understand what they said in this particular situation. The Grom 98 plan was something that was implemented by peacetime units within a peacetime set-up. There were predictions that there might be an aggression, and under the law on the army, on the VJ, one was now to declare one of these so-called extraordinary state of situations in order to give the army a chance to prepare for what might follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The last thing you said is not really an answer to my question, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, he's I think now three times said no, and if you want to persist in using your time on this, that's a matter for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You testified about General Ojdanic's vigilance, his attempts to ensure that he was kept aware of the activities of the units in the field in Kosovo, and I think you'll agree with me that where army units are deployed in the vicinity of civilians it is very important to keep a close monitoring of what they're doing. I'd like you to have a look at 3D -- what we call 3D484, and I'd like to ask you to comment on something in it. Page 14 in English. And this is page 14, second full paragraph, in the B/C/S copy. And it -- in the English copy this is a continuation of what page 13 indicates General Dimitrijevic was saying. No 3, and I quote: "Number three, about the discrepancy between the Pristina Corps, the army, all the way to us here, that's obvious. I think that so many unusual incidents and a lot of what's going on in the Pristina Corps are precisely the consequence of I'm at liberty to say the alienation of a corps commander and with him the command of the VJ both from the 3rd Army and the General Staff." I take it that General Dimitrijevic here is speaking about unusual incidents happening in Kosovo in the Pristina Corps resulting from the alienation of the corps commander. His command from the General Staff. Now, this is dated the 10th of December, 1998. And if we look at page 15 in the English copy, middle of the page in the English copy, which is also page 15, the second to last paragraph in the B/C/S copy, we see that General Ojdanic said: "With regard to the conduct of the Pristina Corps, the problem is broader, and allow me some other people present here --" sorry, "and allow me and some other people present here to analyse some things and try to resolve it like soldiers and men. It concerns not only the Pristina Corps but also the 3rd Army command. I can't say it before this audience but yesterday I analysed it thoroughly." Firstly, do you know what General Dimitrijevic was speaking of when he refers to unusual incidents occurring in the Pristina Corps and resulting in the alienation of the corps command of the 3rd Army command from the General Staff. Do you know what General Dimitrijevic was speaking about?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is presented here is a personal belief put forward by General Dimitrijevic. He probably got some special reports through bodies that he was working with. I don't have any reliable information on that, nor indeed could I say that there was any sidestepping the chain of command at any level. So I was at the collegium meeting. I'm familiar with the position that he presented, but I don't think it's possible to confirm what he says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. But General Ojdanic we see acknowledged the problem in saying that it was broader, and said that he would try to resolve it like soldiers and men. Do you know what, if anything, General Ojdanic did to resolve this problem that he acknowledged?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you, an order is much easier to issue than to implement. When you implement an order, especially when it comes to terrorism, there are a lot of unknowns.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question is whether you know what General Ojdanic did to resolve the problem.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't say. I don't know. But I suppose he spoke about what the levels were and what the problems were that needed resolving.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you don't know, then it's for Mr. Stamp to pose another question. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Let's move on to P931. That's the collegium minutes of the 2nd of February. And if we could go to page 15 to 16 of the English version. I think you will have to read it, because it's the bottom of page 15 to the top of page 16 in the English, and it's near the top of page 14 in the B/C/S. The second paragraph from the top of page 14 in the B/C/S. This is Major-General Andjelkovic speaking, and he says: "My next question concerns the competence of the army. If it is true that the subordinates are doing what they shouldn't be doing, and sending us reports saying that they did not do it, and we have quite adequate and accurate information that they did do it and nobody has been held responsible, I cannot accept that." Do you know what General Andjelkovic was speaking about here?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think at the level of the General Staff we did everything which, if there were actions that constituted significant aberrations from the order then measures were taken. And as I said a while ago, it was the position of the General Staff, of the chief, and I can show you that, it was requested, it was demanded that no random actions would be allowed and nothing that strayed from the regulations. And the Presiding Judge mentioned a while ago that an army is always based on discipline, and it was said as General Ojdanic was adamant later on tasks were to be carried out in detail and orders that were issued had to be implemented in the strictest possible way, and that is the essence of what Andjelkovic said. So if there is something somewhere, then measures must be taken no matter who this is about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was there a situation arising where persons were behaving improperly and sending incorrect reports about what they had done and nobody was being held responsible? Is that a problem which arose?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the reports that were arriving at the General Staff from subordinate commands there was no information to indicate that. There was sometimes information and, yes, it was said quite rightly who should be doing what if there was anything like that. However, what eventually reached the General Staff in terms of reporting, whoever had a responsibility in the chain of command was duty-bound to take measures. What eventually reached the General Staff in those reports, there were no such cases mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: But that is precisely what General Andjelkovic was saying, that the reports were not reporting misbehaviour, but they had information that the reports were incorrect. Do you know what was done by General Ojdanic about the situation?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said a while ago that as for the level of the General Staff, and this includes General Ojdanic, demands were made that we were to receive completely accurate reports down to the lower -- lowest possible level. Nothing was to be done without the General Staff being informed about the situation throughout the units in its entirety, and that is why in August, among other things, the purpose of our visits and touring the units was to ascertain what the actual situation was and to establish the reliability and authenticity of the reports that we were receiving and if there were any discrepancies in terms of what the situation was. As I said, in August the General Staff took a team to Kosovo and Metohija. The tour took three days. Among other things, the purpose of this was to during the unit and see what the situation was in terms of any of the various elements of combat readiness and to make sure how the tasks were being carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can I ask you this: Is it then that General Andjelkovic was saying that the reports, official reports coming from the units in Kosovo were not to be trusted necessarily on the face of them about the conduct-- or let me rephrase that question. Is it that General Andjelkovic was saying that reports emanating from the units in Kosovo were not necessarily truthful about the conduct of these units?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think -- I don't think the General said anything about Kosovo with regard to these reports. I don't think Kosovo is in there anywhere. I think that's a misleading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is going to -- unless I read the two or three pages before, that is going to be, I think, a question of looking at what the General said in context and could be cleared up by re-examination if I'm taking out of context. But I think if one reads all of the report it is clear that they're referring to the units in Kosovo, an operation in operative zone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question doesn't necessarily depend on the reference being to Kosovo, does it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In indeed it does not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Therefore you can pursue the line without referring to Kosovo and we with read the whole document and see the context in which General Andjelkovic was speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Do you understand the question, General, or would you like me to repeat it? The question was Andjelkovic was telling his colleagues at the collegium minutes, including the chief of General Staff, that the reports emanating from the units in the field were not necessarily accurate in respect to the conduct of those units?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Andjelkovic spoke about all the reports reaching the General Staff from all the formations, all the armies, not just from Kosovo. This wasn't just reports about combat activities. These were all sorts of reports. As far as I know, he was -- he was an assistant for electronic technology and signals. It was probably something from that area, from his area. They were being -- they were facing problems in that sector. So possibly it was something about that too. It wasn't just problems in Kosovo. What was being discussed in the collegium meeting is the overall situation in the army and all the strategic groups not just the 3rd Army or just the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That was the 2nd of February, 1999. Can we look at --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before you -- if you're moving off that, I want to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Obradovic, one could be forgiven for thinking that something prompted Major-General Andjelkovic to raise the issue of crimes being committed by members of the army and reports being sent which did not disclose that. Are you saying that did not happen in the meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I'm not saying that wasn't discussed. I think Andjelkovic is right. It wasn't just about crimes that may have been committed in Kosovo. There were other activities during which crimes were possible, cases of misuse, looting, overall crimes, and that measures were to be taken and were taken. And I'm trying to focus here on sector that he was most familiar with, so I assume that he had information on something else. It's very hard for me to tell you now what General Andjelkovic's focus was meant to be when he was saying about -- when he was talking about these things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You were present at the meeting, were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Overall I attended all meetings of the General Staff collegium whenever I was in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you mentioned just now his area of responsibility. What was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Andjelkovic was one of the assistants of the Chief of the General Staff, and he covered electronics and signals, a system that ensured the effective work of the command system, and subordinate to him were the units in both peacetime and wartime ensured that the electronic equipment and communications were in good working order. And this applied to the units under his command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now please think carefully about what he is reported as saying, that the next question concerns the competence of the army. If it is true that subordinates are doing what they shouldn't be doing and sending reports saying that they did not do it, "...and we have quite accurate information that they did do it and nobody has been held responsible, I cannot accept that," now, that looks as though there was something specific that was troubling him. Can you recollect what it was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't say. It seems that he was being quite decided on this. So it must have been something from his own area for him to be this firm about it. It had to be something that he was dealing with and was privy to. I believe it was something from his sector, from his area and one of those units. That is my present assumption for the simple reason that I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You can't remember about this. Okay. Thank you. Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we proceed to P938. And this is minutes for the meeting of the 18th of March. And I think we could first look at page 10 in the -- in the -- sorry, page 11 in the English copy, which corresponds to page 10, paragraphs 5 and 6 in the B/C/S copy. And then General Dimitrijevic speaking. He says: "With respect to that, too, the theory that the MUP and the army are conducting mopping up operations of the territory are exceptionally widespread. Every morning I read very carefully and in great detail the Pristina Corps combat reports, and there was not a single case where we were conducting something; instead, they are always attacking us and we return fire. "I propose that we should discuss that here at the General Staff level at least; even if not everyone should know everything, I think that you more than anyone should know the real truth, because you are the -- you are the personalisation of the whole institution. Something is not right here." There again, we see General Dimitrijevic suggesting that the reports coming from the Pristina Corps were not necessarily accurate about the activities of the corps. Is that a correct conclusion, that the security chief of the VJ was saying that these Pristina Corps reports are not necessarily accurate about the activities of the Pristina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The thesis advocated here by General Dimitrijevic, as you can see he received this information from some sources in the West, so this thesis is very present in the West that the MUP and the army are conducting mopping up operations. That's the theory. And it's a fact that the Chief of the General Staff and the collegium as a whole insisted on knowing the full truth of the situation in the units. So what General Dimitrijevic is saying is nothing new. It's not that we didn't want to know or didn't know. There was no reason for us not to trust the subordinate commanders and the subordinate commands. We had no reason to doubt each and every piece of information we received. We had no reason to think it was unreliable. It would have been -- and it doesn't matter whether we're talking about the 3rd Army, the 2nd Army, the Pristina Corps, or any other unit. These were responsible and able officers, and there was no reason to doubt their reports or to think that what they were reporting was untrue and not correct or that there was something else going on that they did not report on. There had to be controls and visits to make sure that the reports were correct, and this was done. So we were able to confirm all the facts that arrived in the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, if we look at page 25 of the same document -- I don't think I have the reference in B/C/S, so I might have to just read it. General Ojdanic said, and I'll read it to you, sir, it's the last paragraph of page 25 in English: "All the major decision regarding the use the army in accordance with the authorisation from the competent body that is the president of the FRY that commands the army in peace and war. I am not talking about details, it is obvious that something here is not right and I will call and talk to the 3rd Army commander about that, and I also think that should be followed by him coming here so that we can sit down and talk properly about this subject." So that would not be an attack on someone but a proper conversation. Do you know if any steps were taken in regard to any of the problems that were arising in the 3rd Army and General Ojdanic referred to here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, page 23 on Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, this paragraph that my esteemed colleague is reading from should be read in its entirety by the witness before he answers because I think the context is important to what General Ojdanic was talking about there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, the witness is reading it. That I would say is not an appropriate comment, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it may be helpful in the long-run if you just read the whole paragraph to yourself, Mr. Obradovic, and then Mr. Stamp will ask you his question. What's your question, Mr. Stamp? THE PROSECUTOR:

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: General Ojdanic is speaking about matters within the sphere of the 3rd Army command. And I'm not right and these were matters that were covered at this collegium meeting. Do you know what if any steps General Ojdanic took in respect to the command of the 3rd Army to resolve these issues?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't had a chance to read the entire document, but I can draw a few conclusions. The task was by means of analyses, assessments, and so on to discover what problems there were in commanding, because there are certainly always errors whenever anything -- any kind of work is being carried out. So the purpose was to provide assistance to those who may have had difficulties finding their way in all this. So what is being said here is that there was anything wrong this should be discovered and assistance provided if necessary. In early March General Ojdanic headed a team from the General Staff as the Chief of the General Staff to visit the 3rd Army, see what the problems were and solve those problems with the army commander. So he went directly on the -- on to the scene of the events to see what was going on, to provide assistance, and to see that problems were solved at each level of command. That was the gist of it, and that was what this control was all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, he said any other rampage without the knowledge of the corps commanders must be prevented at higher levels. Do you know what he was talking about when he said any other rampage?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Rampage. Well, it's a little rough this term. It refers to failure to carry out tasks according to plan. Any deviation from the task or failure to complete a task, well, the term he used, "rampage," is not really a good one but that's what it refers to, and it might refer to it an individual or a group, but simply no one was allowed to act on their own according to their own ideas and will. That was the standpoint of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Now, apart from visiting the 3rd Army and offering assistance, did General Ojdanic do anything else to correct these perceived problems in respect to the command of the 3rd Army?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the purpose of the control was not only to talk to the commander, it was also to visit the units, the units on the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. It was a numerous team according to all its elements so that apart from the Chief of the General Staff all the other organs did whatever they could to see how tasks were being carried out, to see what the problems were, to assist in solving these problems, and to make sure that the appropriate action was taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: What we want to know, General, is we have two situations, February and March, where General Ojdanic indicates that he would take steps, he would do something to rectify the problems that were identified in respect to the 3rd Corps. I just want to know if you know of any steps that were taken to rectify these problems. That's it simply.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally cannot confirm this in any specific terms. The Chief of the General Staff, the army commander, the corps commander, he spoke to them personally. I as a member of the collegium was not aware of the details, but as a function of command and within his sphere of competence if any measures were needed I am sure he took such measures, because I can tell you that General Ojdanic was very firm and that all orders had to be carried out regardless of who was involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just a brief remark. I think that this was not a fair question. Mr. Stamp said that both in February and in March General Ojdanic said he would do something, but I don't see any reference here for February. Only General Andjelkovic was quoted with reference to February. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, it was actually December and March, but I think the witness understood what I was saying, Your Honours. Those are the last questions I have on this topic, and I would want to move on to something else. I don't have much long left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Obradovic, did the visit to the 3rd Army take place before this meeting that we're looking at?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The visit to the command of the 3rd Army took place in early March 1999, and the team was headed by General Ojdanic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, this -- this meeting was on the 18th of March, so are we right to assume that the visit was before this meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And in the paragraph we've been looking at, General Ojdanic says: "It is obvious that something here is not right." Can you tell us what he was referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I couldn't say. I don't know what specifically he was referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could it have been a rampage without the knowledge of the army and the corps commanders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I disagree with the term "rampage", because were the army to go on a rampage it would be outside the command system, and in our case the chain of command functioned at all levels. If these were individuals --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So does it follow that what was wrong -- or what he described as "something is not right" must have been within the command structure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I couldn't confirm whether it was in the command structure or in the units. I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what he was referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the -- the comment by Mr. Visnjic and Mr. Stamp's response that it was not particularly material whether he said February or March or December and March is really quite significant, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I agree with you and it's a matter you will no doubt wish to resolve. The -- if Mr. Stamp can't formulate the questions properly, then it's very difficult for us to make anything of the answers. But if you wish to clarify it in due course in your own re-examination or cross-examination, that's for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Mr. Obradovic, we have to have a break at this stage. That will be for half an hour. Please leave the courtroom with the usher, and we will resume at 25 minutes past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: General, are you familiar with the 37th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That was part or attached to which corps, do you know?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning a part of that unit was resubordinated to the command of the 3rd Army and later to the command of the Pristina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: And do you know the 211th Tactical Group? Do you know that unit?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 211th Tactical Group they were from the 211th Armoured Brigade but based in Nis. It was a unit belonging to the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Most of your evidence yesterday, General, was in relation to the efforts made by the army, the General Staff of the army in particular, and yourself for cooperation with the KVM. Can I just ask you a few preliminary questions in respect to the KVM? You said over a period of time it became apparent to the army that certain members of the KVM were siding with what you call the other side, that is, the KLA, and you were shown collegium minutes in which examples were given, including lending active assistance to the KLA. Were the persons who were members of these KVM, monitoring groups, or so engaged, identified at all?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on a number of indicators contained in the reports, we drew the inference that certain members of the verification mission were acting in a biased manner, but they took one approach to the MUP and the army and a different approach altogether while dealing with the other side. There were situations where they strayed from the terms of the agreement governing the OSC and NATO mission's work in Kosovo and Metohija. Individual cases were cited, especially in the analysis conducted by General Dimitrijevic, that individual members of the verification mission were doing things that were not within the framework of the agreement and were practically siding with the other side. They were supplying them with weapons and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: These acts of assistance, particularly supplying them with weapons, were there who were allegedly involved in supplying the KLA with weapons identified?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm saying is something else. There were supplies of weapons coming in from Albania and other areas, and they did nothing to stop this. They did nothing to cut the supply lines, the weapons being smuggled from Albania and other areas into Kosovo. They took a rather benign approach to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Did you have information or did General Dimitrijevic say that KVM members were involved in supplying arms to the other side?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His conclusion was that they were making it possible for them to get supplies of weapons. I think he even said something about foodstuffs and victuals. As to the exact manner in which this was taking place, well, that's a different thing altogether.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yeah, well, let's focus on supplying them with weapons. You could just answer that yes or no. Did General Dimitrijevic or anybody else furnish information that the -- that individuals of the KVM were supplying members of the other side, the KLA, with weapons?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. That wasn't what was said, that members of the mission were doing this directly. They were making it possible for the terrorists to do that, and they were doing nothing about stopping them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. I have -- I have it here that you said earlier at page 43, line 14, that these were acts of assistance, particularly supplying them with weapons. Were there -- who were allegedly involved in supplying the KLA with weapons, and you said -- sorry. I should go to the line before that because what I'm read something a question of mine. You said in line 13: "They were supplying them with weapons and so on and so forth." So I take it that that is not correct, that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The witness has made that clear. Please move on, Mr. Stamp. He very quickly changed that to explain that it was their failure to intervene and stop supplies that was what was in issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was it your position that the KVM was entitled to inspect VJ facilities and barracks?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The agreement said that the focus of the Kosovo Verification Mission was to monitor cease-fires, monitoring movements by the army and activities taken by the army, but this did not include checking the units that were in barracks or counting the men or the weapons. Under the Vienna treaty this was under the subregional arms control. Therefore, each weapon such as heavy artillery or perhaps equipment belonging to the armoured units, all the equipment or weapons belonging to the air force, that included all of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can you have a look at P -- not P, 4 -- or 3D484. While it is being brought up, can I just ask that question again. Was it your view in 1998 that the KVM were entitled to inspect all the weapons of the Pristina Corps and to verify the situation in all facilities? Was that your view in 1998?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't just my view. That was what the agreement envisaged. And you saw the order of the Chief of the General Staff yesterday control of units in barracks or along the border cannot be exercised without special approval from the chief of General Staff. I said that yesterday and it's not my intention to repeat it today. As for everything else, control was possible within the -- under the terms of the agreement. This question was based before the relevant authorities to see what the political position was and whether any changes would be introduced that might affect this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That answer does not appear to be consistent with what was said before so it needs to be clarified. The question you were asked was, was it your view in 1998 that the KVM were entitled to inspect all the weapons of the Pristina Corps, and you said that was what the agreement envisaged. Did you mean to say that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, they had the right to check the units but not to enter the barracks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I thought you'd earlier said that checking of the arms, weapons, fell under the Vienna treaty.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Major equipment that fell under the Vienna treaty. The rest was something that the verification mission had access to. All the equipment, all the manpower including weapons but with the exception of the barracks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Speaking of the barracks, can we look at page 12 of -- of the document before you. This is the collegium minutes for the 10th of December, 1998. The last paragraph of page 12 in English is also the last paragraph of page 12 in B/C/S. You could probably take a look at it and I'm just read it while you -- you said: "General, as for the situation down there now, there are now about seven, eight hundred of them divided into four zones; in accordance with valid documents, they have the right to ask to inspect all weapons of the Pristina Corps and its entire composition in all its units and to be allowed to verify the situation in all facilities, including the use of special equipment and for a more reliable data collection." Was it your view in 1998 that they would have the right to verify the situation in all facilities?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is about the entire composition of the Pristina Corps or access was granted for purposes of control except the barracks. Once again, the verification mission was allowed to check the entire composition of the corps, as well as its weapons and other equipment. The only thing they weren't allowed to do was to get into the barracks. Some of them were adamant that they should go into the barracks and see the offices and everything else. You know what there is inside a barracks, don't you. But this was not under the terms of the agreement. So for this task to be verified this is something that required a special political decision and an order from the General Staff. I suppose this was -- if this had been verified or, rather, resolved, there would have been no reason for such a task received by the army not to be implemented. There was nothing special really being concealed in the barracks or anything that would have been of any particular interest to anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Was it the -- was it also, and this is just to be clear, the position of the General Staff, of General Ojdanic in particular, that the VJ ought to deliver reports about the arrival and departure of units in Kosovo to the KVM?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. That position was clear. That was the position of the General Staff and General Ojdanic, and that's what we did. All movements of units in Kosovo or to Kosovo, if that happened the verifiers were notified. I explained yesterday that one of the major tasks was the replacement of soldiers that was regulated in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
