utterances.text: Thanks. I think you have answered what I was asking. And lastly, General, since the VJ liaison, or at least the relevant organ of the VJ did receive reports from the KVM; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no special liaison organ through the chain of command. We got operative reports from subordinate commands, and especially there was a team in the Pristina Corps for relations with the verification mission that submitted reports to its superior command, the command of the 3rd Army, and the liaison team that existed in the 3rd Army submitted reports to the liaison team in the General Staff, and that's the one that I headed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, but do you know whether or not the OSCE mission sent reports to your Ministry of Foreign Affairs?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that because that was not within my line of work. All information that was discussed at the federal commission, well, there was information and probably -- or, rather, I assume that there were such reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, if we look at P941, that is the collegium meeting of 25th of February, 1999, and it's English e-court page 23. The corresponding B/C/S being also page 23, second paragraph. General Dimitrijevic said: "I wanted to say something to Obradovic. I cannot agree that they do not send reports. The OSCE mission is sending daily reports to our Federal Ministry of Foreign Affairs. The federal ministry of foreign affairs then analyse these reports once a week, sometimes within a shorter time and make a summary. In other words, they are supplying daily reports to our government." So General Dimitrijevic told you there were reports being provided. Did you make an effort and did you ever see these reports?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information that General Dimitrijevic received in this connection, well, I mean from his point of view he probably did receive some information. I said a few moments ago that I did not have occasion to see such a report, and I told you that at the federal commission when the situation was analysed there were discussions concerning some information that I assume was related to the reports that were submitted to the Foreign Ministry from the OSCE mission in Kosovo. I did not have occasion to have such reports. I did not receive copies, not from the mission and not from the members of the Federal Commission that was headed by Mr. Sainovic. But there were discussion on certain issues that probably included military reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: When you learned that these reports were being forwarded by the OSCE mission, did you seek to get copies of them in the capacity of your role with the OSCE missions?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If these reports were there, had there been anything interesting concerning the army or had there been any problems with the army or in terms of the relationship between the army and the mission then I guess would have received that. However, I assume that there was nothing significant from the point of view the army. That is why this was not submitted to me and nothing special was said to me. Then I could have made the chief of General Staff aware of some problems if something like that had been presented.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well. You say -- you said on more than one occasion that in 1998 General Perisic said that the units that were withdrawn could be returned if the other side were not complying with the provisions of the agreements. Is that -- is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said that, and I was a direct participant in the talks between General Perisic and General Clark when this problem was discussed, and he told him that he did retain that right, that if the other side did not observe the agreement, he retained the right to have the units returned in the area where they had originally been.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Is it your position that on the basis of any of the October agreements and the UN Resolution the VJ could return any of these units unilaterally without consultations with the OSCE mission?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not one-sided. This position of the chief of General Staff was accepted by General Clark, and he promised that he would guarantee that that would not happen. He just said if that happened, or if that were to happen, if the other side were to abuse this and not honour the agreement, he retained the right to return part of the units to the area. That was the agreement with General Clark, who accepted that he would make sure that the other side abided by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, but what I want to know is is it your understanding that on the basis of some agreements, any of the agreements, the VJ could return units to Kosovo unilaterally based on their assessment, their own assessment, without any consultation with the OSCE mission?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Yesterday I stated that the army as a whole observed the agreement, the provisions of the agreement as a whole, and the Chief of General Staff insisted that as far as the military was concerned the provisions of the agreement should be completely abided by to the very letter. No one-sidedness was to be permitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: The 37th Brigade that we spoke about earlier, was that based at Raska?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 37th Motorised Brigade was basically stationed in the garrison in Raska.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Where is Raska?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The garrison of Raska is in the territory of the Republic of Serbia. To explain it to you in greater detail, south of Kraljevo, about 60 kilometres south of Kraljevo. From the administrative border with Kosovo, say 20 or 30 kilometres away west of Mount Kopaonik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I see. Can we have a look at P2039, please. This is a report on the 20th of March, 1999, to the Pristina Corps command, and copied to the 2nd Army, Uzice Corps command, for information, as you can see. And it says that: "On the 7th of March, 1999, the 37th Motorised Brigade departed to the general area of Kosovska Mitrovica with the aim of carrying out exercises and raising combat readiness." So this brigade was brought into Kosovo, not to the edge of Kosovo as we heard about earlier, according to this document. Do you know whether that was reported to the OSCE verifiers?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you look at the date, it was the 23rd, 1999. In that period the verification mission was withdrawing from Kosovo. It says up here command of the 37th Brigade, strictly confidential, the 20th of March, 1999. This is four days prior to the NATO aggression, and it has to do with the standby forces, with the peacetime forces. So the verification mission during the 19th and the 20th left Kosovo, and I think that you know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes. What the document shows is that there were -- they departed the general area -- departed to, sorry, departed to Kosovska Mitrovica with the aim of carrying out exercises and raising combat readiness on the 7th of March, 1999, when according to what we're hearing it would have been your obligation to advise the OSCE personnel who were there prior to this or around the 7th of March. Were the OSCE personnel or monitors advised about this augmentation of the forces inside Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was part of the forces, a smaller part of the forces- as you can see, the size is there- that were on the rim of Kosovo. And in view of the overall situation that prevailed, that there was an immediate threat of war -- or, rather, of bombing, measures were taken for part of the units to be brought to the rim of Kosovo in order to be able to oppose the aggression that ensued. I've already said that every activity of units in Kosovo was something that the verification was -- verification mission was notified of, so it wasn't that there was anything unknown.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Kosovska Mitrovica is inside Kosovo, the territory of Kosovo, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Kosovska Mitrovica is in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Not the rim.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, approximately close to the administrative border. It's not a big distance, but it is in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Okay. Could we -- well, you have to answer the question, really, before we move on. I think you're -- it's implied that your answer is no. Do you know of the OSCE monitoring mission being advised of this movement of troops into Kosovo to -- for combat readiness and to augment the forces already in Kosovo? Do you know of them already being advised of it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that it was our obligation to send notification of any movement within Kosovo towards Kosovo concerning Kosovo to notify members of the mission, and they had been notified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The question here's a very simple question, Mr. Obradovic. We've got your evidence about where this group of troops was moved to. The question is: Was notification of this particular movement sent to the Kosovo Verification Mission, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Even though the troops, according to you, were not moved into Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not say that they covered that area. That area where the unit was sent was in the territory of Kosovo. I mean, this unit was sent to train in the broader area of Kosovska Mitrovica. That indeed is area that belongs to the territory of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Obradovic, you said plainly to us just a short time ago that they were on the rim of Kosovo, indicating that they had not gone into Kosovo. Are you now saying that on the 7th of March they did go into Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The rim of Kosovo means something that is close to the administrative border of Kosovo in the territory of the Republic of Serbia. That's the rim of Kosovo. The area of Mitrovica is in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Very well, then. Well ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we have a look at P1967. This is an order dated the 20th of March, 1999, signed by General Lazarevic, and it's an amendment to the decision on supporting the MUP forces and breaking up and destroying terrorist forces in the area of Malo Kosovo. And this was at a very, very crucial time, I think you'll agree with me, the 22nd of March, 1999. And it is headed "Joint Command for Kosovo and Metohija." Now, as Chief of Operations, had you ever had seen an order or orders for operations in Kosovo sent by the Joint Command. And it is dated the 22nd of March, 1999. Had you ever seen any such orders?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Such orders and this command in the chain of command did not exist from the point of view of the General Staff that I worked at at the time. I was still in the General Staff then. This date is roughly two days prior to the NATO aggression against the federal republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Can we look at P2808. This is an order of the 16th of February, 1999. It's also signed by General Lazarevic. And if we look at page 9 of this order. And this is page 4 of the B/C/S version of the same. General Lazarevic orders that the -- and there is some handwriting here, but that the group 211, and that is the group that we referred to earlier, the 211th Tactical Group shall be subordinated to the Pristina Corps by a special order. Was the 211th Tactical Group -- well, I think you will agree that the 211th Tactical Group was a group from outside of Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This temporary composition at Tactical Group level was from the armoured brigade that had been stationed in the Nis garrison, and the order is what it says at the end, that that unit, according to a special, order would be resubordinated to the Pristina Corps according to a special order when an opportunity for that arises. Otherwise, it was stationed in the Nis garrison.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: That is all I have in cross-examination. Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Obradovic, on Tuesday you told us. That the war plan was drafted and then sent to the Supreme Defence Council, and you described that as the top echelons of the state, and you then said when approved it was approved by the president of the republic. In dealing with this war plan what was the composition of the supreme Defence council.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the Supreme Defence council at that time it consisted of the president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, the president of the Republic of Serbia, and the president of the Republic of Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When the war actually began did the composition of the supreme Defence council change?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The composition of the Supreme Defence Council did not change because the members were there ex officio. The presidents of the two republics that comprise the federation and the president of the federal republic. If a new person were to come to one of those positions, then by virtue of the office he held he would become a member the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did the way in which it functioned change when the war started?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know the Supreme Defence Council did function on the whole. There were some thoughts along the lines that the member from Montenegro did not often attend Supreme Defence Council meetings. I cannot confirm that for you, though, because I did not have an opportunity of receiving such information nor did anybody tell me any such things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the expression "Supreme Command"?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That term was used when the state of war was proclaimed. There was the president of the republic. He commanded the army in war and peace and then it went without saying that the Supreme Defence Council as the Supreme Command -- well, this member of the Supreme Defence Council who was the head of state was the commander-in-chief but basically the commander-in-chief was the Supreme Command -- the Supreme Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Obviously you're familiar then with the expression. If the Supreme Defence Council was effectively the same body in war and peace, can you explain why it had a different name in wartime?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Supreme Defence Council functioned in war and peace. In peacetime it was called the Supreme Defence Council, and once a state of war was declared it grew into the Supreme Command. That's what it was called. Otherwise, it is the Supreme Defence Council that practically commanded and decided on how the army was to be used, in accordance with the constitution and law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And just to be absolutely clear about this, what was the composition of the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Supreme Command, as I've said, were those three members that were on the Supreme Defence Council. When the state of war was declared, the General Staff also joined the Supreme Command as the staff of the Supreme Command. It grew into a body that was of an operational nature, as a staff, if I can put it that way. The chief of General Staff ex officio was chief of staff of the Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerman, I was advised that you may seek leave to cross-examine the witness at this stage. Is that the position?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is, just on matters raised by Mr. Stamp that were not part of the original examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, does that trouble you?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: I'm not sure what he's referring to, matters that were not part of the original examination. Would he just say precisely what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, can you elaborate a little?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Of course I can. Your Honour, during the direct examination of this witness, Mr. Visnjic made no attempt to develop evidence against my client, General Pavkovic. When Mr. Stamp started his cross-examination he did by going into issues regarding the plan for operations in Kosovo and Metohija, the remarks made by General Pavkovic at the interdepartmental staff meeting, whether or not the Grom plan was ever actually implemented. That gets into whether General Pavkovic was operating with or without authority as has been contested in this case. And just to -- just to clarify the matters as much as possible --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think you've said enough for our purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, anything else you want to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, I have nothing to add.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. This is one of these situations in which it's possible that there would be a miscarriage of justice were we not to modify the normal rule and allow cross-examination in view of the way in which the Prosecution have cross-examined the witness. So we will allow further -- well, I don't think you crossed at all, so we will allow you to cross-examine the witness on the matters that you've referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I want to say before I begin for the record that I have pending a motion for partial severance and if that motion were to have been granted I would have no questions, and so I'm now going to go forward just in absence of that being granted for the protection of my client in the event it is not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You will appreciate that the timing of the motion is such that it's not been possible for us to deal with it by this stage. We have to allow appropriate time for response.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I wasn't being in any way critical to the Chamber for not deciding it. I know it will be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It will be done promptly I can assure you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I appreciate very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: General, my name is John Ackerman. I represent General Pavkovic in this case, as you probably concluded from what was just said. I want you to look first at a document that you looked at when Mr. Stamp was questioning you, and that is Exhibit 4D137. And that should appear on your screen in a moment. We'll start with the very first page of that document. What you see there is that 28 July 1998 directive of General Pavkovic that -- or General Perisic that has -- that we've been talked about so much. The first thing I want to draw to your attention is -- is the language right at the very top. General Perisic characterises this directive as a "Directive to deploy the Yugoslav army for securing the state border with Albania, units and facilities in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija and crush the armed rebel forces." So that is what he says is the purpose of that directive; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That's the gist of the directive issued at the level of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, if you look down at the bottom of that page there's a paragraph, it might be on the second page of B/C/S. It begins with "The foreign factor deems the present activities." Do you see that paragraph? It's the last paragraph on the English -- English on page 1. We're too far with the -- there. It's that paragraph in English. "The foreign factor." And I don't know where it is in B/C/S. I think we've got it. Yeah, it's the fourth paragraph down on the first page. And what Mr. Stamp asked you about that, or asked about it, and there are -- I think there are two ways to read that, correct me if I'm wrong. One way to read that is General Perisic is saying if we deploy -- the present activities of the Yugoslav army is justified, but if we deploy in a different way, then that would be an inappropriate use of force against innocent civilians. That would be one way to look at it. The other way to look at it is he's saying is the NATO and the -- the other parties are looking for some pretext to make a claim against us before the United Nations and doing something like this might very well give them that kind of a pretext, not that it would be a use of force against innocent civilians, but they might very we will make that claim while we're making this pretext. Would that be a fair way to interpret that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you asking me, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the analysis that was present when this directive was issued, that the foreign factor can interpret this as is stated here, that it's excessive use of force, that bringing fresh forces into Kosovo is being done to use them against civilians, whereas what was really going on was a fight against terrorism, which is why the title of the directive is to crush the armed rebel forces. And the fact that this could be misused, that's something quite different.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. I want you to look now at II, which is, I think, on the second page of B/C/S and English. It's right at the very top there. You'll see it. Now, General Perisic there is talking about the use of the Yugoslav army up to the point of this order. He says the army has, in line with the situation, undertaken specific measures, intensified the securing of the state border toward the Republic of Albania in the zone of the Pristina Corps in-depth security has been provided, intensified the security for military facilities and units in Kosovo and Metohija and ensured a regular supply flow to the Yugoslav army units for the execution of their task. Throughout its presence and by carrying out the training in the entire territory of Kosovo and Metohija, the army has had a repelling effect with regard to the Siptar terrorist forces and it has offered direct assistance to the forces of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia. Now, it's the case then, isn't it, that General Perisic certainly knew how the army had been used up to that point, that it had been used to offer direct assistance to the forces of MUP, and it had been doing training on the territory of Kosovo and Metohija outside the border belt, which had a repelling effect with regard to the terrorist forces. So it appears that he was fully aware of the operations of the army up to that point; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Based on this it can be concluded that the Chief of the General Staff was aware of all the activities of the army and not to repeat things, the gist of it is what is stated here. The Chief of the General Staff knew what was being done inter alia in the area of responsibility of the Pristina Corps on the territory of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then he says in the period up to now, the Yugoslav army has successfully carry out the assigned tasks. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The conclusion is, and in this directive it says that in the period up to now the Yugoslav army has successfully carried out the assigned tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And at no point in that paragraph about the Yugoslav army's deployment up to that point does he say that there was anything improper or illegal about it, does he?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's quite clear. If this is the conclusion of the Chief of the General Staff, one should not doubt this conclusion, because based on this the further directive for the deployment of the army was issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, I think there is some confusion regarding this order, and you were asked numerous questions about it today, and I think the confusion lies in this: This order -- this directive contemplates two stages of deployment, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would say not two stages of deployment but two stages of engagement of the forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's a fair statement. You're right. And the -- the reason there are two stages is there were one stage -- there was one stage of engagement for that period of time when there was no declaration of imminent threat of war or emergency or actual state of war, and that was first stage. That would be carried out during that time. If it got to -- the situation got to the point where there was to be such a declaration, then stage two would come into play and there would be a mobilisation and then it would be the active part of that directive. Is that fair statement?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. If the situation were to change radically, the armed rebellion in Kosovo or the terrorist actions in Kosovo could grow into an armed rebellion, and in that case mobilisation would be carried out to raise the army to a higher level of combat readiness, but for this to be done one of the states envisaged in the constitution, such as an imminent threat of war, would have to be declared.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So then if you look at under III there, you'll see first of all some language about the first stage, and then you'll see language about the second stage. And Mr. Stamp referred you to a paragraph at the end of that which says: "The readiness in the deployment areas is 17 days upon the receipt of the mobilisation signal at the latest." That refers, does it not, to the second stage where there would be a declaration and a mobilisation and not to the first stage of that directive?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When mobilisation is declared the mobilised units, the reserve of units, are not capable of being used in combat right away. There has to be a certain period of time depending on the circumstances and the unit itself for the unit to be trained and enabled for use in combat. So it's a little over two weeks here for these mobilised units to be prepared for use. The reserve forces, as soon as they're called up, they can't take up weapons and go out to carry out a task on the very same day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, on line 17 he said yes, and then said when mobilisation is declare. The word "yes" didn't make it into that answer. So the first word in line 17 should be "Yes."

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, if you look back up at the first stage, what General Perisic says there is: "Through quick actions coordinated with the forces the MUP of the Republic of Serbia, overwhelm and destroy the sabotage and terrorist forces in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija as per a special order from the General Staff of the Yugoslav army." Correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that was a directive for rather immediate implementation of this first stage, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's a directive that was intended for what was to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That isn't terribly clear to me, so perhaps you can clarify that, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm doing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Stamp asked you whether you've ever seen any kind of a special order from the General Staff with regard to that, and I would direct your attention to 3D702. Now, this is a one-page document dated the same day, 28 July, 1998, and it's directed to the 3rd Army and refers to the Grom 98 plan, and it orders General Samardzic in the 3rd Army to draw up plan for the engagement of the forces in two phases, first and second, and orders him to submit that plan by the 3rd of August, which is like five days after the issuance of his rather comprehensive directive; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And that indicates a -- rather than some kind of plan that's going to be put on the shelf for much later use it indicates some urgency on the part of General Perisic that this matter be rather quickly implemented, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As soon as the Chief of the General Staff verified and signed or approved the plan for the commander of the 3rd Army it entered into force and implementation could begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, let's look very briefly then at -- at 4D140. On the very next day, 29 July, after the issuance of the directive, 29 July, under the heading "Grom 98," General Samardzic issues this document. And rather than being a directive, this document is an order, isn't it? And it's an order to smash sabotage and terrorist forces and armed rebellion forces in Kosovo and Metohija; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is a directive, and as you can see the document of the command of the 3rd Army takes the form of an order. The command of the 3rd Army issues a decision and issues an order detailing how the task is to be carried out. And as you can see in the upper right-hand corner it's connected to Grom 98 which is a title emanating from the General Staff. So the two documents are connected.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And you said during your earlier testimony that there would be -- in the normal course of events there'd be a map associated with such an order. And you can see right under that first designation of the purpose of the order that there was in fact a map and it sets out sections of the map and what it was about, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told His Honour that this kind of document is accompanied by a map, and here it says that the map is 1:200.000 and the sections are enumerated so this covers the overall area of the army and it would show how the forces are deployed. So the map of deployment would be a significant attachment to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, the document we're now looking at, 4D140, is it an original document in B/C/S, or is it a copy? It looks original.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You'll see the stamp and everything on it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And it would be -- to this document there would be a map attached rather than 3D703. Is that the position?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think the what the witness said was the map tends to flow down through the chain of command. So this going from the 3rd Army to the Pristina Corps would carry the map with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, you say that you were going to produce to us a map. Does that relate to both of these exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I haven't got the map in my hands so I don't want to be really specific with you about it but I believe I have the map that's referred to in this document signed by General Samardzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you think it is the original one signed by him or a reconstruction?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It appears to me to be the original one signed by him, but I can't be certain about that either. I think it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, if you'll look at paragraph 2 of this document, which is on page 3 in the English under the heading "Army Tasks." And it's page 3 in the B/C/S, second paragraph. General Samardzic basically repeats under the tasks he's assigning to the Pristina Corps he basically repeats the language of General Perisic in a coordinated action with Serbian MUP forces launch rapid attacks to smash and destroy terrorist forces in Kosovo and Metohija in accordance with the special order of the General Staff of the Yugoslav army. Now, when he uses the language "the special order," he's not referring to some future special order but one that's in existence, and this actually puts everything into play, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If the situation develops in a negative way, the Chief of the General Staff will issue a direct order that the implementation of this task begin. It was not necessary to write a special order. The Chief of the General Staff would simply say go ahead, and this is how things would have to be done in breaking up the terrorist forces on the territory of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But in the first phase that was -- that was immediately implemented. It's the second phase where if there had to be mobilisation there would be a delay and additional orders; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The order applied to the second phase practically, the second stage. If this situation were to change more radical measures would have to be taken at the level of the General Staff and downwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Okay. I think you -- I think you're looking at a different part of the document than I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Yes, because I was just about to observe that the part that was just read out to the witness was a part under the first phase.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: In which the witness said in respect to the special order that the Chief of the General Staff would if the situation develop, issue the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think the witness is looking at the language under the second phase and what I'm referring to is that language with regard to the first phase.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Are we correct, Mr. Witness?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Now, I want to take you down further in the document to paragraph 4, and that's on page 5 in the English and page 5 in the B/C/S. General Samardzic uses the language here, "I have hereby decided." Can you tell us what that means in an order like this when he says, "I have hereby decided"?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When one receives an order and when an overall assessment of the situation is made, the situation in which the unit currently finds itself, when the opposite side is evaluated, their own forces, the commander in charge issues a decision in the form of an order. He orders what is to be done next. That means that he has decided how to further deploy the forces to carry out the task.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's not something you'd find in an order that's designed to be carried out at some later date, but it's in the form of a "do this now," isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. When it says that a decision was made, that means that what is topical is to have a task embarked upon. That's what he means when he says that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, do you want to break now or do you want to go on a little long? It's up to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If this is convenient for you we'll break now. We'll break for lunchtime, Mr. Obradovic, so would you again go with the usher, and we'll resume at 1.45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.45 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: General, I want to continue with the document we were dealing with, and I now want to take you down to the language right before paragraph 5, which is on page 6 of the English version of the document. And it's also page 6 in the B/C/S, at the top. Now, you recall that above this point General Samardzic was setting out the tasks, and then at the bottom you'll see this language. First of all for intensified and in-depth security of the state border and protection of military facilities immediately which means he wants that carried out immediately, does it not?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then --

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's about securing the state border in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then the other part of his -- the tasks that he set out for sure road passability and smashing the terrorist forces he orders that commence on the 6th of August at 0500 hours; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was one of the tasks, that is to secure that the roads could be travelled because of the need to supply the units and other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So the bottom line of this is this is an action order. It's not just some plan, is it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Essentially this is an order, yes, an order as an element of command, and this can be seen as an element of command. And the plan of deployment for the forces is normally attached to an order.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, over the lunch break I had all of the maps we had brought from my office so I could try to find the map that we were talking about. However, unfortunately it appears that that is a map we don't have, but I have a map that I'd just like to show to the witness so that he can identify it and so that Your Honours can see what it is we're talking about and then we will conduct an immediate search for the map that was attached to that order. If that would be helpful to you. I don't need to go into it unless you think it would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I doubt if it's helpful, Mr. Ackerman if it's simply being displayed as an example.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, this actually is an action -- a map that was attached to an order it's from the 10th of August, 1998, and it deals with what -- what maps is from that large map that's approved as I understand it and the witness can confirm it or not, what happens is then smaller maps for made for each individual action that's going to take place and those are also signed, and this one you'll see deals with an action taking place at Ratis, and it carries the signature of Dusan Samardzic up in the upper left-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you pass that over here it might be the best plan.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right and if you need the witness to verify that's his signature and what I'm representing it to be I think we can do it. I think it's pretty clear that's what it is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the attachment that normally follows an order by the army commander where he approvals this. There's his signature. As you can see, this is a map of 1:200.000 is the ratio, and you can see how the forces were deployed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Who wrote the date on it, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I wrote the date at the top, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Ackerman, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's in remarkably pristine condition to have been the original map attached to the order, and I have to make it clear to you I've had previous experience of seeing maps reconstructed for presentation in this courtroom, not in this case. And it may be quite important for us to distinguish between those that are originals and those that may have been reconstructed to present the picture as it was previously.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: When I find the one that we were talking about this morning, Your Honour, I'll make sure we have adequate information regarding its provenance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Meanwhile we shall return this one to you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think they're likely distributed in more than one copy, Your Honour, so there maybe one that's kind of been beat up and there may be more pristine copies of the same document. But I'm not positive about that, but we will clear it up if we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You may have to do it through a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's what we're working on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Now I'd like you to look at another document. This is P2166. And this is also a document that was referred to by Mr. Stamp when he talked about things that were said by General Pavkovic at a meeting of the interdepartmental staff for the suppression of terrorism on 2 November 1998. The part that I want to draw -- well, let me ask you a couple of questions first looking at the first page. This is -- this meeting is clearly a secret meeting, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I have no information on this meeting. Therefore, I can't say what this is about, except for what I just read.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Please look at the top of the -- of the document. Doesn't it say "State Secret," with a stamp there?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Defence, state secret." This means that there is a certain degree of secrecy that attaches to this document, and you can see this is highest possible degree of secrecy.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So a document like this wouldn't be going off to the Official Gazette or the news papers or anything like that, would it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Documents like these are kept in a special way and are not published.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, it wouldn't follow that the meeting was necessarily secret. The record may well be.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The persons who were present at that meeting, there weren't any persons outside the government there, were there? There weren't any reporters or persons from other countries or anything like that? These were all people from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia that held high positions; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the list of those who attended I have to conclude that this is the highest ranking possible state and military leadership. On behalf of the army I think there was the Chief of the General Staff, the chief of the security administration, the army commander, and the corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The remarks of General Pavkovic begin on page 2 of the document, and I want to take you through those down to something that he said on page 3 of the document, which is right before he starts setting out the tasks that were contained in a plan that he refers to. And I think on -- in the Serbian version it's that's also on page 3. It's right in the middle of your screen. It should be. Kasto [phoen]. According to this General Pavkovic says: "As may be concluded, our plan was not to kill all the Siptars or expel them from Kosovo and Metohija but to destroy the main terrorist forces and separate the terrorists from the people." And then goes on to speak of the plan: "Pursuant to the decision adopted it at the 5th session of the Supreme Defence Council on 9 June 1998, the law on the Yugoslav army, the defence law, and the rules of service of the Yugoslav army, a plan to suppress terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija was drawn up which provided for the engagement of units of the Serbian MUP and the Yugoslav army." Now, this plan that he speaks of there was created on 9 June 1998, and is a different plan from the Grom plan that we've been talking about today, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Well, if he could be directed to the [indiscernible] created on the 9th of June, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It was the decision of the supreme Defence counsel on June 9, 1998. I might have misspoke. I don't know how long after that decision the plan was created.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you answer that question, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was that a question for me? I didn't get it. One can infer based on this that in the beginning of June the Supreme Defence Council considered --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Mr. Ackerman will ask his question again, and please focus on the specific question that's asked. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The plan that this talks about here is not the same plan as the Grom plan that we were talking about earlier today; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Now I'd like to look at P938, page 25 in the English, and 23 in the B/C/S. And you were also referred to this earlier today by Mr. Stamp. Mr. Stamp was referring you to that paragraph that begins with: "All the major decisions regarding the use of the army ..." And goes on. According to this, General Ojdanic said this: "I'm not talking about the details, it is obvious that is something here is not right, and I will call and talk to the 3rd Army commander about that, and I also think that should be followed by him coming here so that we can sit down and talk properly on the subject. So that would not be an attack on someone but a proper conversation. However, you need to be careful, in my knowledge what is done in practice is a response to what had been done." And then he goes on to say this: "The army cannot very well stand idly by if a military vehicle with two officers is hit, two colonels are wounded and it should just pass on. The army, together with MUP, has to undertake some measures if the purpose of blocking and searching the terrain and likewise, if someone is discovered there, they should be attacked. I think that we all agree about that, but any other rampage without the knowledge of the army and the corps commanders must be prevented at higher levels, and with respect to that, I think that the best remedy and solution is to do it as soon as possible." It appears, doesn't it, that what General Ojdanic is talking about is a situation where terrorists attacked a military vehicle and hit two colonels who were wounded and is concerned there was not a proper army response to that situation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could both the witness's microphones be switched on, please? The interpreters can't hear him. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just stop, please. Your microphone is not on, Mr. Obradovic. You can start that answer again once it is. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is stated here that when things like these are happening, when terrorists are attacking and there are losses and casualties the army should not stand idly by and do nothing about it in the sense of blocking, taking certain areas, tracking down the terrorists forces and crushing them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Now, it was at this point that Mr. Stamp asked you about -- said to you that he now suggested a couple of times to you when General Ojdanic said that he would take care of a problem, and he told you that one of those was in February and one was in March, and then when objection was made he said, well, actually, it was in December and March. Now, there's a significant difference, is there not, between December of 1998 and February of 1999 in that in December when there was a problem that needed to be taken care of the 3rd Army commander was Dusan Samardzic; right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. As early as December 1998, the army commander was General Samardzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And I don't know if there's any connection, but you know that very shortly after he said that he would take care of that problem in December General Samardzic left the 3rd Army.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, it was late in 1998 and early 1999 that General Pavkovic was appointed commander of the 3rd Army, thus replacing General Samardzic, but I can't remember the exact date. And perhaps it doesn't even matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And then the second thing that he asked you about that General Ojdanic was going to take up with the 3rd Army commander was the one we've just looked at, and that's the one where the army was not taking what he thought was an adequate response against terrorists but letting things go by when these two colonels had been attacked and wounded, being correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This view of his was in reference to the commander of the 3rd Army at the time. That was General Samardzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let me make it clear that I read that completely differently from the proposition you've advanced, Mr. Ackerman, that General Ojdanic was concerned about an incident, and what had happened was that the army had allegedly overreacted to the attack on its officers. Now, is that not -- not only a more -- an explanation more consistent with the whole text, but if not, equally valid with the one that you're advancing?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think not at all, Your Honour. If you look at the one sentence, "The army cannot very well stand idly by --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed and that's because -- he's explaining that he's got to deal with this in a delicate way because he appreciates that the army had to take very firm action against a terrorist attack, and if they went too far then he understood to some extent why that would happen, and therefore he would have to approach it diplomatically. Surely the whole thing has to be read together.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And not in separate sentences.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It is look at the next sentence he's saying the army and the MUP have to get together and do something about this. They can't just let terrorists just attack the army and kill colonels without taking appropriate response.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed. It's the same, he's just following it up. He's saying he understands actions have to be taken. However that's an matter for argument at a later stage. I thought it simply important that you should know that I certainly don't at the moment read it the way you're suggesting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, in the world of reasonable doubt, it probably is good enough.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp, have you any further cross-examination arising from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: If I take you back to the collegium minutes -- thank you very much, Your Honour. I do thank you for proper for that. Collegium minutes of the 10th of December 1998, 3D484 where I asked about what did General Ojdanic do in respect to the complaints or the concerns, you were just told actually by Mr. Ackerman that this was in reference to the 3rd Army commander and that General Ojdanic was not the 3rd Army commander at the time. General Pavkovic was not the 3rd Army commander at the time. When I looked at it again, is that General Ojdanic said at page 15 with regard to the conduct of the Pristina Corps, the problem is broader and allow me some people present here to resolve some things and resolve it like soldiers and men. It involves not only the Pristina Corps but also the 3rd Army command. Can I ask you who was the commander of the Pristina Corps at that time, do you know?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the end of 1998 it was General Pavkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before we lose track of it, page 78, line 14 there is something missing there my recollection is at present. I don't read it the way you're suggesting. Please continue, Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: You were shown 3D140, and I don't think I need to show it to you again, which was the draft order prepared by General Samardzic. Now, that draft order was prepared in response to the directive by General --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me there was no evidence that it was a draft order. That an active order that was signed and everything. There is no evidence that's a draft and that's a misstatement of any evidence in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: First of all the document I think is 4D140 and not 3D, and secondly my note is the order had been drafted by Samardzic. Now, is this not in fact, Mr. Ackerman, an order which Samardzic has to send up the line to have approval given to it by the map being signed?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I don't think so. If might be in any event it's not a draft it was an act.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Ultimately it is. The system as I understand it - I better clarify this with Mr. Obradovic - but the system as I understand it, Mr. Obradovic, is that the 3rd Army commander writes out the order he expects to be given and what he intends to order those under his command to do, and he passes it up to the General Staff and there it's approved and returned to him and he acts on it. It's the same document but he acts on it once it comes back to him with approval. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, essentially as soon as is a decision is approved on the map it's signed off. This document is verified and it's used to work based on that from there on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Thank you. I have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic. I'm sorry, Mr. O'Sullivan.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: With your leave I'd like to ask some questions that arise out of your questions to the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: These ones just now or earlier?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The ones earlier that you posed directly after the first cross-examination by Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Please do that now before Mr. Visnjic re-examines.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: My name is Eugene O'Sullivan and I represent Mr. Milutinovic I'd like to ask you some questions that arose out of the questions put to you by the Presiding Judge earlier today. To give you some context, as I understand your evidence, you became the assistant head of the sector for the operations and staff activities of the General Staff in July 1998. Have I got that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, by decision of the president of the federal republic I was appointed assistant Chief of the General Staff of the sector for operations and staff activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: And the date you started that function was July 1998; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I reported to my new post on the 10th of July. I asked the Chief of the General Staff at the time to grant me a couple of days off so that I could deal with some private problems concerning accommodation for my family because my family back at the time was still in Podgorica. So officially I took up my duties on the 17th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Thank you. The Presiding Judge asked you about the war plan, and I'm -- for the record I'm looking at pages 141 -- sorry, 14981 to 14920 of the transcript. And you had told the Chamber a couple of days ago that the war plan or, as you call it, the plan of use was a pre-existing plan, a plan that had come into existence before you started your functions in July of 1998. Is that -- am I correct on that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The war plan was made earlier on. It was approved, verified considerably before I came to work in the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Do you know what year that might have taken place, when that war plan was elaborated, in what year? If you don't know that's fine, but if you do, could you tell us?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not tell you exactly what the time was because I was in the command of the 2nd Army as chief of staff then, so I cannot tell you for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I'd like to ask you some questions about the expression Supreme Command, and my question is this: Are you aware and can you confirm to us that the expression Supreme Command is not provided for in the constitution of the FRY or the law on the VJ or the law on defence or the rules of service of the VJ? The expression "Supreme Command" does not exist in any of those texts. Are you aware of it and can you confirm it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. What you said just now is correct, that in the documents you refer to there's no specific reference to the existence of a Supreme Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I'll move to one last area of questions. General, the evidence in this case is that on the 23rd of March, 1999, the Supreme Defence Council held a meeting. The position of Mr. Milutinovic is that after the 23rd of March, 1999, and throughout the period of the state of war in 1999, the Supreme Defence Council, that is the presidents Milosevic, Milutinovic, and Djukanovic, did not meet. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. O'Sullivan, before that question's answered what is the basis in the evidence for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I can refer the Chamber to Exhibit 1D35.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which says.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Which is a submission made by Serbia-Montenegro in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's a submission which is not yet part of the evidence in the case and may yet not become part of the evidence in the case. And is that the sole foundation for that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: That is -- well, Your Honour, it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Milutinovic has chosen not to give evidence, so we need to a basis for the question you're putting to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, I would -- I submit that's -- well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm not saying that the line you're pursuing is inappropriate, but the way you're doing it I think is and that question should be rephrased.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, this -- this is an exhibit on our 65 ter list, and we rely on it and this witness perhaps can confirm it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Confirm what?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Confirm that there were no meetings of the VSO. He may be aware of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's a question you can ask without putting that document specifically to him I would have thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I believe I had put the question without the document first. You asked me if there was a basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Very well, continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware that the Supreme Defence Council, that is Presidents Milosevic, Milutinovic, and Djukanovic, did not meet after the 23rd of March, 1999, nor at any time during the state of war in 1999? Are you aware of that? And if you're not, that's fine.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To be quite precise, on the basis of what I know, I went late in March, the end of March, to become commander of the 2nd Army. When in mid-April I got orders on resubordination of the MUP forces to the army, I got a reply from the minister of the interior of Montenegro that one of the conditions, why conditions were not created for the MUP to be resubordinated to the army is due to the fact that president Djukanovic was not taking part in the activities of the Supreme Defence Council. That is the only thing I can confirm. That is what I have in writing from the minister of the interior of Montenegro. It had to do with President Djukanovic and his statement to that effect. Now, whether it was actually was that way -- well, I'm just saying what was contained in that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the interests of justice I would like you to look at page 13 of document 4D140, because I think the record needs to be accurate with regard to what this document is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we have it on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Page 13, please. We don't need the B/C/S version, I don't think. Unless we need to ask the witness a question about it. It's page 13, please. Where the signatures are. There it is. Your Honour will see at the end of this document there are two things. It contains attachments, composition and strength of combat groups, decision on the map for phase 1, decision on the map for phase 2. It is typed in five copies and delivered, past tense, to the Pristina Corps command, the Nis corps command, the 203rd MABR command, 202nd POB command, Pristina VOK command. Nowhere does it say it was sent to the General Staff for approval. This was an order that was signed and stamped and sent out that day and there's no question about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, ask the witness that question, please, or if you prefer, I will ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: General, I think you heard my representation regarding what happened with this document. I'd like you to look at that page that has the signature of General Samardzic on it. It indicates there how it was distributed, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A document that is made this way of this document of the commander of the 3rd Army is made is submitted to subordinate commands. As stated here these are the command of the Pristina Corps, of the Nis corps, the command of the 203rd mixed artillery brigade, then the 202nd brigade that was also submitted to that army, and number 5 the Pristina command. Those are the units that received orders from the 3rd Army with the signature of the commander of that army, General Samardzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Obradovic, did this document or would this document in accordance with normal practice go to the General Staff for approval before the orders were issued to the various elements of the army referred to at the bottom of that page?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, we should clarify this. The commander of the army explained his decision in a timely fashion in terms of the engagement of these forces, and he got approval from the chief of General Staff. Once he received this approval, then this task was being implemented. As we can see from the order of the commander of the army, we see that the order with the attachments were submitted to the subordinate commands and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please don't repeat yourself. Does that mean that you're saying that the document we have on the screen did not go from General Samardzic to the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judge, when the commander of the army came to explain the decision, then usually his plan would be made in two copies. One copy that would be approved would be given to the commander of the army, and the other copy would remain in the General Staff. So what the commander of the army sent down the chain to his subordinate commands was not sent to the superior command on the basis of the decision of the superior command he made his own order and sent it to his subordinate commands as we can see here as attached.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So are you saying that the plan, which was in two copies, must be a different document from this?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The plan that was done in two copies was not in the army command. There is the order and that is map attached. On the basis of that order then excerpts are sent to the subordinate commands through this kind of order as stated here. This approved order signed and sent to subordinate commands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But who approved this order?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was signed by the commander of the army, as you can see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm misunderstanding your reference to approval. So to be absolutely clear, you're saying -- are you saying there is a document, another document, that is the plan which was in two copies and was approved but isn't part of the chain of command? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This fully exists in terms of command. The chief of General Staff issued a directive, and then the commander issued --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please, please, just tell me whether there are somewhere in the world two copies of a plan on the basis of which approval was given for this document then to be issued by General Samardzic.

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are no two plans. There is one order that was defined.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I -- Mr. Ackerman, can you help us further? I just do not understand this. I don't know what the two copies were that were discussed with the army one of which then had the map attached to it if it's not this document drafted by General Samardzic for approval so that he could then proceed with that approval to give commands as specified.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document was -- was drafted and sent out the day after Perisic issued his directive. It clearly was distributed, as this witness has said, to the various commands shown at the bottom. Now, what intervened between the time Perisic sent his order which would have gone probably instantly from Belgrade to Nis and when this was finally issued the next day I don't know but it may very well have been an approval by Perisic orally or something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In the normal course of things orders issued by commanders of the 3rd Army and Pristina Corps and places like that don't get approved before they're issued. They're issued and copies go up the chain and if somebody finds a problem with it then they deal with it but if you had to send every order you were going to issue up to the General Staff to get approval before you issue it you couldn't fight a war. Things have to happen quickly, not through all this bureaucracy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Obradovic, if what Mr. Ackerman has just said is correct, this document that we're looking at would not be submitted to the General Staff; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the army explained his decision to the chief of General Staff. When that was approved, then through the order he regulated how the order would be carried out, how the task would be fulfilled, and that is what you see in this order here sent to the subordinate commands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And he wouldn't send a copy of this even for the record to be kept with the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At his own level he keeps a copy. One copy remains in the army command. And excerpts are sent to subordinate commands as you can see here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the plan that was approved was simply what he told the Chief of the General Staff. There's nothing in writing that shows what the plan was on the strength of which he was then able to issue these orders?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see why there is a confusion with plans. Attached to the order is the map on which we see the plan of engagement of forces what is referred to here is some special plan. So the order is the main document that regulates the way in which the task will be implemented. And on the map one only represents the engagement of forces in terms of time and place. How -- which forces will be engaged in carrying out the task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Obradovic, your evidence to us is that there was a directive on the 28th of July and that there was this document, this order, on the 29th of July. Now, the directive did not authorise this order. The directive required plan to be submitted to the General Staff. Now, am I misunderstanding that?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In essence the director of the General Staff was drafted and done or, rather, sent on the 28th. The command of the army when they received this directive of the 28th worked on it, that is to say on assessing the situation, on assessing the overall situation, and then they wrote an order as we can see here. That was defined on the 29th, what you are asking me about now. That was written on the 29th on the basis of the directive of the chief of General Staff that had been made a day earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was there then a map attached to the directive?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the General Staff usually -- well, since the General Staff does not give direct orders to units at textual level there was only the directive in written form as a written document. There was not graphic representation on the map from the General Staff. The decision on the map for the engagement of forces is done by the commander of the army, commander of the corps, lower levels.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: May I, Your Honour, since this is re-examination? I know we have spent a long time on this, but I'd just like to ask him two questions just to clarify something which I thought was clear, but now I'm not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Arising from what?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Arising from some of the answers he just gave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Could you look quickly at 3D702. That's a one-page document. Order to the 3rd Army command and the heading is Grom 98 in the top right-hand corner, and it says: "Draw up the plan of engagement of forces on coordinate named Grom 98," and it goes on in paragraph 2. In paragraph 3 he says: "Submit the plan of engagement to General staff by 3rd of August." Now, the plan that we're seeing here that you were just discussing, was this plan signed by General Samardzic on the 29th? The plan that he was ordered to submit to the General Staff by the 3rd of August?

utterances.speaker: MILORAD OBRADOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you can see here, the director of the chief of General Staff made it obligatory for the army command to act immediately upon receiving the directive to implementing the task, inter alia assessing the situation and preparing documents for the implementation of the tasks involved, and that is why it is written here that the commander of the army is asking for approval of that decision of his on the 3rd of August as envisaged here, or, rather, that he do what the chief of General Staff ordered on the 3rd of August.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Obradovic, the question you were asked was a very simple one. There's an instruction in this document to submit the plan of engagement by the 3rd of August. Now, what was that plan of engagement and was it submitted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, the approval of the plan, that is to say the approval of the plan that the General Staff should know what the idea of the army commander was, how he thought he should carry out the task and to have this plan of his approved in terms of engagement of forces in accordance with his plan and the graphic representation on the map. So this has to do with what the army commander defined in his order of the 29th of July. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can you deal with the question? Was that plan referred to in paragraph 3 submitted to the General Staff? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When this plan was approved one copy should have remained in the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let me go back and ask the question, and please don't avoid answering it this time. Was the plan referred to in paragraph 3, in documentary form, submitted to the General Staff? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The commander of the army explained his decision on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you understand -- do you understand the idea of answering yes or no? Was the plan referred to in paragraph 3 of this document submitted to the General Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it was. I think that one copy of that plan should have remained in the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's not the question we're asking you. The question is was it submitted?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand what you're asking me, what the core of the matter is. Once the decision of the commander of the army was approved, then it came into force, and the commander of the army, once he obtained this approval, went back to carrying out the task.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Obradovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's be clear that there's not an interpretation problem here. You have the document of the 28th of July in front of you. Would you read aloud point number 3.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 3: "I shall carry out approval of the plan of engagement of forces on the 3rd of August, 1998, at 1100 hours in the GS of the army of Yugoslavia."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
