utterances.text: Well, that explains it all at least in part. It clarifies it, because there's no order to submit a plan. I apologise to you for getting so impatient, but I was proceeding on an English translation which is inaccurate. Mr. Stamp, do you have any further questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: No, nothing further, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Obradovic -- oh, sorry. Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I just have something to note in relation to an exhibit that was used yesterday during the cross-examination carried out by the Sainovic Defence. It is the minutes from the collegium of the General Staff dated the 30th of October, 1998. In stating what the exhibits that we will be using -- we said that we would just use it to present to the witness. We stand by that. So we do not want those minutes of the 30th of October to go into evidence. We are not going to tender them. We have done what we intended to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STAMP
utterances.text: Your Honours, I had indicated that I would like to have a look at it because we did not have translations of the entire document. I think to understand the context of the document and the context in which the questions were put it would be prudent if the Court would accept into evidence the collegium minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may be of assistance. We are not opposed to having the document admitted into evidence. We just wanted to be consistent in terms of what we had originally announced. So if the Prosecutor believes that this is the way to proceed and if the Trial Chamber is of that opinion, we are not opposed to that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, it will be admitted into evidence. Well, it will be marked for identification at this stage until it's translated, and -- I'm reminded that it's not as simple as that. We don't just hand over documents here. It has to be uploaded into e-court and that's in your hands Mr. Petrovic and what you will be required to do is upload it immediately so it gets a number and then you will have to make a filing so it will be translated so it can be properly admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That will be done, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Obradovic, that completes your evidence. Thank you very much for coming here to give it. You're now free to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. I wish to thank the Prosecutor, and I wish to thank all the lawyers on the Defence teams.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Before we proceed to the next witness I want to raise with counsel issues that arise from the delayed production of expert reports. As I understand the position, the witness Prsic will not be called. The report of the witness Stankovic was filed on the 9th of August. The record of the witness Jokic was filed on the 4th of September. The English translation for the report of Simonovic has been uploaded into the system. That for Stankovic has not, and -- although it is available, as far as I'm aware, and there is no information available to us about the translation of the report of Radinovic. Now, can someone bring us up-to-date on these because it will probably be necessary for us to make an order about the running of time in relation to the reaction to these reports. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can address the two that I am responsive for the Stankovic and the Simonovic. It's interesting both translations are in e-court but there is some issue that the Stankovic one has not been released. My -- it has -- the latest I have is that Stankovic has been released we have a filing prepared for the Stankovic report to give notice that it's available, that should be filed this afternoon. The -- we are preparing a similar filing for the Simonovic report. However, my cursory review of the translation has found at least two significant errors of translation. So don't know whether in -- I had planned in the filing to at least bring to the attention of the parties those two that I had found and then I don't know whether there are more. Obviously I only had a few moments in court to leaf through it and I found, for instance, instead of RJB the translation is RDB, which is a completely different service, but I think that one should be easily remedied just by giving notice to that in the -- in the submission. So those two are both available in English for what they're worth, and they will be filed, I guess, by the start of business tomorrow, formally being tendered to the opposing side. So how -- how the Court wants to set the timing for the other things that need to be done pursuant to the rules is up to Your Honours, but that's the situation with respect to those two reports for which my team was responsible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, our understanding is that Stankovic has in fact been distributed to the other Defence teams.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's correct, because it's a joint -- a joint -- a joint expert. We are preparing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But -- but that's the one you say you're concerned about the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No. Simonovic the other one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And it's my understand that both are now -- both are now in e-court and they are released which means they can be accessed by the parties although we have not formally given notice of that we plan to do so this afternoon with respect to Stankovic and this morning with respect to Simonovic I can identify that 6D668 is the Simonovic translation 6D670 is the Stankovic translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 6D668 and 6D670 for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And who is responsible for Radinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: My colleague Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, can you help me out on that?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the translation of Mr. Radinovic, Professor Radinovic's expert report according to my information has the deadline of the 15th of September. I would like to also use this opportunity to inform you that another translation request was submitted by the Defence team an annex to this report. It contains three elements, one being a number of technical errors that occurred during the drafting of the first report, and this includes several exhibits which were simply omitted, were not attached to the report, which is something of course that we'd like to do and will do. The other thing being supplementing the report by a couple of footnotes. Professor Radinovic added a number of other exhibits that had been presented throughout the trial so far. I do have a proposal for Chamber. This is something I was going to propose earlier on. By your leave and in cooperation with the translation service the CLSS, we might be able to amend this document and do a better translation so that we have a -- a -- we have the report and the annex as a single document. Obviously we would be filing a written request to have to done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There isn't time though to start this exercise all over again, Mr. Visnjic. The 15th of September sounds to me like a date when the whole lot can be translated and available. What you are referring to as supplementary material does not sound very extensive.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You can consider that and decide how to approach it, but I think you would be well advised to discuss the situation with CLSS and see if that can be a shortcut to compiling one report including the additional material. What we shall do is deal with the ones which are available in a written order and deal with the final one when it is available. So it's important, Mr. Ivetic, that these filings are made forthwith. Thank you. Now, your next witness, Mr. Visnjic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, our witness number 4, General Branko Gajic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Gajic. Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading allowed the document you now have.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. There's no need to take anything out of your briefcase unless it's spectacles or something. That's it. Thank you. We found a number of witnesses bringing documents out of brief cases and putting them away religiously every time we break and never being referred to them start to finish, so let's try to avoid that. You're now going to be examined by Mr. Visnjic on behalf of Mr. Ojdanic. Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I am partly to blame for some of these witnesses because I told them they should keep their 92 ter statements in front of them at all times just in case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you issue the matching briefcases as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, good afternoon. Could you please state your name for the record?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: I'm Branko Gajic. I was born on the 17th of July, 1944. I'm a Major General of the VJ in retirement.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. General, before we start with your evidence, I want to ask you if it's true that you made a statement to the Ojdanic Defence team which you signed on the 17th of August, 2008 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. And if I may just additionally explain something. There was an investigator who spoke to me on the 8th of August. I wanted to raise certain objections about some substantial matters in that statement, so he corrected those, and after that I was ready to sign the statement which finally happened on the 17th of August.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As far as I understand the date on page 1 of the statement is the 8th of August, and the last page we see the date of the 17th of August 19 -- 2008; right? So this is what accounts for it.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Is it true that as you were preparing for your evidence here you looked at the statement?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you confirm that everything in that statement is true? Were you to testify about these same matters here in the courtroom you would give all the same answers would you not?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, let me just ask you one thing, please. Let us make a short pause between questions and answers. It is necessary so that the interpreters are able to distinguish who said what. Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Visnjic, what is the exhibit number for the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I was just about to say that. 3D08 -- 1084. 3D1084.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is Mr. Gajic's statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, what's your profession?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: I'm retired right now, but I used to be an active-duty officer until my retirement.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And your rank at retirement was?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Major-General.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What were your responsibilities throughout 1999 and -- 1998 and 1999?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Until the 27th of April, 1999, and previously throughout 1998, I worked as assistant chief of the security administration and I was also the deputy chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: And your rank at the time was?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: I was a colonel and remained in that rank until the 16th of June, 1999, when I was promoted to the rank of Major-General.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I won't be going through all the details of the witness's role or job. This is something you can look up in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, in view of your post, the post that you held back in 1998, were you receiving information about the activity of the Kosovo Liberation Army?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me how you were receiving that type of information?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: It was through reports submitted to the security administration by various counter-intelligence bodies of the VJ. Counter-intelligence bodies more specifically attached to unit commands throughout the VJ and counter-intelligence bodies that were part of the counter-intelligence groups and in actual fact formed a spatial component but in a formal sense they were attached to the security administration. The other way in which we obtained information on the Kosovo Liberation Army was through exchanging information with the Military Intelligence Service of the VJ and also through exchanging information with the State Security Service and the MUP, M-U-P, although to a far lesser extent. It was also through exchanging information with SID, the service for investigations and documents which is attached to the foreign office. We also obtained information from centres for electronic surveillance, military ones. Such information as was relevant for the work of the security administration and the counter intelligence sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. General, were you also receiving information on exchanging data with certain foreign set-ups or groups?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, but rarely. And normally it would be through special channels. For example, through the State Security Service or the investigations and document service of the MUP, but this was on exceptional and rare occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 12 of your statement you tell us about certain contacts that you had with foreign services.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Anything to add about your contacts with the American service?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: That's right. Sometime in August 1997, the then head of the security administration, General Aco Dimitrijevic, told me that people from the CIA were asking to get in touch with us because previously they had already got in touch with the state security sector. The team that arrived in Belgrade, the CIA team, was headed by the then CIA director, and they expressed a desire to make contact with us. This was approved by the General Staff. So we created a platform for those contacts, and I was directly involved in -- in this job. The first contact occurred on the 22nd of October, 1997. It was representatives of the DIA who appears for that first talk, not CIA. This was just an introductory meeting. We were getting to know each other. We were exchanging some basic information about our respective establishments and personnel and so on and so forth. And then at one point they told us that what they really wanted to talk -- those who really wanted to talk to us were the CIA people. We had a total of four meetings, four contacts, if you like, with the CIA, three in 1997 and one in 1998. Those in 1997 occurred on the 14th of November, the 25th of November, and the 10th of December, and the one in 1998 occurred on the 2nd of March. That was the end of it. Our contacts were disrupted unilaterally by the Americans. We never learned why. The way events were to be fold confirmed that we were indeed right and that there must have ban political decision behind this rupture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is DIA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is the Military Intelligence Service or agency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General -- page 103, line 4. The witness said American, American. I do believe that's clear as it is, however?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You mean American Military Intelligence Service?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, DIA stands for Defence Intelligence Agency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, aside from other types of information that you were exchanging at the time, can you tell us what you spoke to the CIA people about? I mean about the Kosovo Liberation Army and the situation in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: If I can just say two or they things about what they wanted to know. They wanted to know about the Islamic factor, especially in Bosnia-Herzegovina. He wanted to know about training centres run by Mujahedin in Zenica, in Doboj, and so on and so forth. And then we also talked about the Kosovo Liberation Army and about Kosovo in general. When we spoke about that, a team that was led by Ms. Bukovski who was head of the unit in the CIA for monitoring the Islamic factor as they referred to it at the time in the former Yugoslavia or the Balkans. We talked about Kosovo, and we talked about the KLA, and we told them that in Kosovo there was being a paramilitary terrorist organisation that was being set up. It wasn't entirely established by this time. It still had the shape of several terrorist groups that normally numbered 5, 10, or up to 30 members, and most of those groups were set up in two areas. One of these areas being Drenica, and this is right in the middle of Kosovo, roughly speaking. It lies along the Pristina-Orahovac-Djakovica road, and the other area was Metohija, the reason being this is where the border belt was facing Albania, which was a very important area, much used by this terrorist organisation. We expressed our concern at the emergence of this terrorist organisation. We said that they constituted a political expression or a political means of a movement of which the final objective was to create an independent state in Kosovo and Metohija. That was stage one. And stage two was probably to create something that I could refer to as Greater Albania. We told them --

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: My apologies. Just slow down a little, please.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: My apologies. My apologies. We also told them that the tear of the organisation was enjoying absolute support in Albania. Albania was a logistics base for them both politically and logistically speaking. It opened its borders to the terrorists, especially after the Salih Berisha's regime had been crushed, which was sometime late in 1997. It was brought down. We were facing great difficulty trying to secure our border because we were unable to control infiltrations and incursions by these terrorists and weapons being brought in from Albania. We also told them that we had information on the links between the KLA on the one hand and the Mujahedin in Bosnia and Herzegovina and other parts of the Arab world, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Iran, that sort of thing. They confirmed that some of our information was accurate. They also said, however, that it was difficult for them to convince those in charge in the US that the KLA was a terrorist organisation. They also underlined that the problem was at its worst among them in the State Department and was being aggravated by an extremely influential Albanian lobby led by Mr. Dole but also by Mr. Lantosh and Mr. Gardi [phoen] and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Slow is down a little please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think we'll need to move on to something that's relevant to the period we're dealing with, Mr. Visnjic. Is there a particular reason why we're getting the history of discussions with the CIA?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, one of the aspects of this witness's evidence will be the activities of the KLA. What I wanted the General to explain for our benefit was the pretext for these activities, and this coincides with the end of 1997 and the beginning of 1998. I don't believe that the General will be dwelling in great detail on these matters, at least based on my conversation with him. I don't believe that will be the case. But as far as I understand, this is a particular stage of the clashes in Kosovo. The previous stage ends, roughly speaking, sometime in March 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What do you -- what do you see as the particular relevance of the activities of the KLA in general rather than their activities in the localities which are the subject of the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, above all, Your Honours, we are trying to say that the activities of the VJ were directly related to the activities of the KLA, meaning the activities of the VJ were for the most part a response to actions taken by the KLA or an attempt to keep them at bay. We are trying to show that in essence the KLA was a terrorist organisation, and the VJ had every reason to use force against them in the way that it was eventually used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That -- all of that is for us ultimately to decide based on facts rather than people constantly saying the KLA are terrorists. It's easy to say and may even be easy to accept, but just the constant repetition of it doesn't take us anywhere, whereas if we get to evidence of events that occur in the areas where -- that the indictment concentrates on then we might get something that's relevant to the issues for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by all means that is what we will be doing. I never thought, and we never tried to focus on this particular part of his testimony. This was just an introduction that brings us to the next stage when we are going to be bringing in a large number of documents that precisely respond to the question that you put to me now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's beginning to sound like propaganda this, so please let's get to the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Very well. General, tell me, you described the sources from which you gained knowledge about the KLA. Can you tell us what your knowledge was about the activities of the Kosovo Verification Mission -- sorry, the activities of the Kosovo Liberation Army.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Well, our first information on the existence of the KLA was received towards the end of 1995, say the beginning of 1996. This information was that in the territory of Kosovo there was intensive work going on in terms of establishing and storage and diversion groups numbering 3 to 5 members up to 10 members, actually. Later on they became stronger, up to 30 members even. In rural areas where the majority population was Albanian, they were being recruited either on a voluntary basis or they were coerced to join the KLA. In these rural areas staffs were being established that command this activity and bring it all together, the activities of all these terrorists groups. In fact, this was throughout Kosovo. In some places this development was slower, in other places faster. That depended on many circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, what was the focus of their activity? Against who were their activities geared?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Primarily towards the MUP; then the army; thirdly the non-Albanian population, primarily the Serb population, but also the Albanian population that they thought did not accept terrorism as a method for achieving political goals. Towards the end of 1997, we had had information that was quite reliable that about 80 per cent of the Albanian population was against armed violence in the attainment of ultimate objectives, namely the independence of Kosovo. That was a problem that caused concern within the KLA and their staffs, so in that period, that is basically all of 1998. With greater or lesser intensity they focused their activities on winning over the Albanian population in rural areas for their own objectives and for the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Tell me, how did this work? What was their strategy?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: They used a wide array of measures. I would like to use the following term "ideological indoctrination," all the way up to methods of coercion that boil down to the following: The method of threats, issuing threats, all the way up to kidnapping, and in some cases they even resorted to liquidation, because in the meantime they established groups that were involved in that only. As early as the end of 1997, they recorded all military-age Albanians, from 18 to 60 that is. In the mean time, they had village staffs. They had a network of village staffs, and they even established illegal prisons. In some places like Smonica in Metohija they even had two illegal prisons in Junik two illegal prisons. They were mostly located in private homes, the homes of people who enjoyed special trust, people who were commanders of these illegal prisons.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Several Prosecution witnesses testified here and stated that in the beginning of 1998 the situation in Kosovo can be subdivided into two periods, up to March and after March 1998. Can you explain to us why -- or, rather, do you agree with this, and can you give us your comment?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes. This period up to March, up to the 5th of March, 1998, is actually linked to the end of 1997 where there was intensive work going on in terms of organisation, but also there was also terrorist activity and armed attacks. I will just state that in 1997 only as far as the army of Yugoslavia is concerned 106 terrorist attacks and armed provocations were launched against them. Fifty-one in the area itself and 55 along the border.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: What is it that happened on the 5th of March?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: On the 5th of March, 1998, in a clash with the security forces a terrorist group was liquidated headed by Adem Jashari of Drenica, who in 1975 had eight criminal reports filed against him. He fled in order to avoid serving a sentence. In the meantime he completed a sabotage course in Albania and then he was an instructor, and sometime in 1996 he returned to Kosovo and he became the head of a strong terrorist group in Drenica. On the 5th of March he was liquidated.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Tell me who took part in this action? Rather, let me rephrase. Did the army take part in this action?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now we move on to the period after March 1998. Can you tell me now what characterises that period, what kind of activity on the part of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: The period after the 5th of March is characterised, to put it in a single sentence, by significant intensification of all forms of activity of the terrorist organisation of the KLA. That is to say from the point of view of organisation, from the point of view of increasing their ranks, forming new terrorist groups, staffs, they focused on the rural areas. The villages, that is. Furthermore, they intensified their efforts to obtain weapons, primarily from Albania where their most significant is sources were, but also from Montenegro and Macedonia or through Montenegro and Macedonia. That is to say that they always had that problem. That was a constant problem for them. So that was one of their main tasks. Furthermore, in their activity they intensified activities against the MUP, namely they attacked police stations. They attacked patrols. They kidnapped individual policemen. They carried out liquidations, and they attacked the army, especially at the border. There were numerous border incidents and armed attacks because the army made it impossible to bring weapons and terrorists in.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, I have to interrupt you. When you say vis-a-vis the army, apart from the border incidents what other kind of incidents were there launched by the KLA against the army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: That's just what I was trying to say. There were quite a few armed attacks and provocations along roads in order to impede communication within the military. Not a single motor vehicle, military motor vehicle could go down roads without armed escorts because they were subjected to real terrorist attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly -- or were you trying to say something else?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Also there were attacks and provocations against units that were combat groups in the area. I'm talking about this period until the October agreement was signed in 1998. There were combat groups in the area, and the KLA attacked them too. As a matter of fact, they did not use only small arms but also recoilless guns, mortars, et cetera. That is say larger calibre weapons. And all of that was really a big risk.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: General, if I understand you well. Let's try to make this bit more concise. The KLA starting in the month of March abruptly intensified its activity to such a degree that it affected the normal work and the activity of the army of Yugoslavia -- or, rather, they even threatened the very functioning of the army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO GAJIC
utterances.text: Yes, one could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think that this would be a good point in time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- For us to break off for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Although we started your evidence quite late today, Mr. Gajic, we nevertheless have to interrupt now because that's the end of our sitting for today, and we will resume tomorrow at 9.00. You should be back here ready to continue your evidence at 9.00 tomorrow morning. Meanwhile, it's very important that you have no discussion with anyone about your evidence or about the evidence in this case at all. Speak to whoever you like about whatever you like except the evidence. Now, could you please leave the courtroom with the usher and we'll see you tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
